speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in following the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who has long experience in military affairs, I do so, of course, merely as a layman but one who has paid some attention to the military commitments and expenditures over the last few years. I shall try to discuss the estimates now before us in the light of the new developments in international affairs, and in the light of methods that might be used in the event of an attack not only on our country but on the countries with which we are associated.
Of course, throughout the country the easing of international tension, to which the minister referred and to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has on occasion referred, and the desire for the control of

these new and terrible weapons, about which we heard this afternoon, have led people to hope that we might be able, through agreement, to engage not only in the control of these weapons but in progressive disarmament.
At the moment the world is obsessed with fear. Fear, of course, is not a good motive for the promotion of international peace; but, as a matter of fact, fear is forcing millions of people everywhere to look for peaceful settlements of current difficulties and disputes.
The terror of the new weapons was outlined by the minister in his speech this afternoon, and as I listened to him I wondered if his department has reviewed the commitments of Canada and the policies of the department in the light of these new and terrible developments.
The white paper indicates the amount of money the people of Canada will be called upon to expend on the army, the navy, the air force, and defence in the year 1954-55. The estimates amount to $1,908 million plus $102 million, which is expected to be a net charge on the special account, or a total of $2,010 million, which is an increase of $208 million over the forecast gross disbursements of $1,802 million for the year 1953-54.
May I just say in passing that I have noted there has been some discussion and indeed some dispute, or so the newspapers tell us, between the Department of National Defence and treasury officers about items which should be charged to this special account. What seems to have happened is this, that when the department has some weapons which are obsolete they are sent to one of our allies as mutual aid, and that enables the department to draw on the special account to pay for new equipment and in that way, incidentally, to escape to some degree control of this house in respect to those expenditures.
The figures in the white paper are stupendous and would be stupendous at any time, but they are certainly stupendous in peacetime; and when I look back over the years and think of the first budgets I saw introduced in this house in 1936 and 1937, budgets of around half a billion dollars, and when I remember how Mr. Dunning used to impress upon the house that it was impossible to raise another ten, fifteen, twenty or one hundred million dollars to give the relief which was so necessary and which was called for at that time by our suffering population, I cannot but regard this figure for defence as stupendous.
Because of the fact that these figures are so stupendous I think it is the duty of this
Supply-National Defence house to see whether they are justified, and if justified, how it is proposed to spend the money.
The minister told us this afternoon that these new estimates come at the end of a three-year period, the period which three years ago we were told would require an expenditure of $5 billion to bring us up to the point where we would be moderately secure, the point where, in co-operation with our friends in other countries, we could expect to feel a measure of real security. But this afternoon the minister told us that we have got to expend this huge amount again this year, and indeed he told us we would have to spend the same amount probably for years to come.
Consequently, it is the duty of this house at the present time to see if the Department of National Defence is really doing the job we expect of it when we appropriate these huge sums of money.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said a few moments ago there had been a revolution in warfare in the last few years. That was pointed out in a very interesting address given over the B.B.C. a short time ago by no less a personage than Sir John Slessor, G.C.B., marshal of the Royal Air Force; chief of the air staff, 1950-52; commandant, Imperial Defence College, 1949; and member of the air council, 1945-47. I would like to quote briefly from what he said at that time:
For the first time in hundreds of thousands or millions of years that man has existed he can carry or propel through the air for thousands of miles, ... a missile that by itself can destroy a city. It is silly to behave as though this revolution had never happened. Actually it has completely transformed the whole complexion and dimension of the problem of peace and war. All previous conceptions have become obsolete.
Let me hasten to say that I am not here to tell you that we can now scrap the navy and disband the army and put all our money on a new model push-button air force. But if there were another major war it would not remotely resemble the last one.
Then in another place in the same speech he emphasized this point when he said this:
I believe the first and most far-reaching consequence of this revolution is that total war as we have known it in the past forty years is a thing of the past. That may sound a pretty rash statement. But I believe it to be true. War is a matter of wills: nations or coalitions went to war to impose their will on an opponent. You started off by trying to do it by persuasion, that is, by diplomacy, and if that was no good you tried to do it by force. At a given moment-the "declaration" of war-you turned over from an interchange of notes between men in top hats to an interchange of bullets between men in tin hats.
The next rather obvious thing I must say is that you did not take the initiative in forcing a war unless you thought you could win it. And (this is
4918	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the important point) we now know to our cost that winning a war does not mean just forcing an enemy to lay down his arms and accept your terms: it means creating world conditions more favourable to oneself than could have been brought about if there had not been a war. Today there is not the remotest chance of anyone winning a war on that definition. A world war in this day and age would be general suicide and the end of civilization as we know it.
Consequently it seems to me that while we are considering expenditures for the defence of our country against the possibility of war, our government, our external affairs department and all the rest of us should be doing everything we can to try to find ways and means of negotiating the difficulties that exist between the nations and of eliminating the possibility of another general war. The world is still trying, of course, to comprehend the tremendous power of the hydrogen bomb as revealed publicly, following the recent tests in the Pacific. Rear Admiral L. L. Strauss, the chairman of the United States atomic energy commission, in a statement made on March 31, 1954, disclosed that one hydrogen bomb could wipe out any city on earth. The power of the atom bomb was measured in kilotons, equivalent to thousands of tons of TNT. The power of the fusion bomb is measured in megatons, equivalent to millions of tons of TNT. The explosive power attained in the March 1 Eniwetok test was estimated at 600 to 700 times that of [DOT]the bombs that destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. These statements are from the New York Times.
Then in a statement issued recently in England by a group of scientific workers- and incidentally they were scientific workers in whose area will be found the great atomic pile of the United Kingdom-they estimated that two to six hydrogen bombs would be enough to break British resistance in any third world war. As the hon. gentleman who preceded me stated, the vulnerable spots- the ports, railway centres and so on-are few in number, and a few of these bombs getting through could put out of the war any country engaged in it.
Then the other important development, of course, is the development in the U.S.S.R. We have been told authoritatively that United States success in producing the hydrogen bomb was largely owing to the material that flowed through the ether from an explosion of such a bomb in the U.S.S.R. and that it made a change in the manner in which United States scientists were working in order to discover that dreadful weapon. Soviet spokesmen have been at pains recently to underline the point that they had these powerful weapons. I should like to put on the record a comment by
[Mr. Coldwell.l

Hanson W. Baldwin, military editor of the New York Times on April 4 of this year. He says this:
The intended import of that (Soviet) warning is simple, that the Soviet union is capable of winning a nuclear war with the United States. This was what Premier Malenkov meant when he said last Monday that any future atomic war "would inevitably lead to the ruin of the capitalist social system," a theme repeated also in communist party secretary Khrushchev's speech the same day.
It is generally agreed that while the existence of the H-bomb is a very real deterrent in so far as an outbreak of world war is concerned, its deterrent effect is much less in relation to small wars, limited wars or struggles such as those in Indo-China, Malaya, street fighting in Trieste, Israeli-Arabian border clashes, etc.
Thus we see that the obligations of Canada and the other countries in connection with the requirements of the United Nations, NATO, and so on, are not altogether eliminated by any deterrent effect the H-bomb may have. However, I believe an examination of the estimates now before the committee will show that little heed has been taken of what Sir John Slessor called this "revolution in war".
It seems clear that the estimates are based upon the second world war conceptions and that the minister has accepted uncritically the huge demands for weapons and equipment that are either already obsolete or become obsolete even before they are provided. I think that point was well illustrated and emphasized this afternoon by the minister himself when he spoke of the huge expenditures for the production of planes in this country and said that they are obsolete before they come off the assembly lines. One wonders whether we would not be far better off by co-operating more closely with the United Kingdom, for example, and by assisting the United Kingdom and allowing the United Kingdom to proceed, for according to published reports she is the foremost aviation nation in the world in the designing of planes. One wonders whether we would not be better off by co-operating with her so that we both might benefit, without our undertaking, on a much smaller scale and in smaller numbers, the building of planes which may become obsolete even before they come off the assembly lines.
Of course military men have always been prone to ask for more than is necessary, and parliament is inclined to grant all their requests because, as laymen, we are not sufficiently informed to refuse their requests. Indeed, if we did, public opinion might view us with suspicion. The public view with suspicion any suggestions-and perhaps properly so-that seem to jeopardize

the national defence against any possible aggression. A prominent member of this house, as reported at page 2810 of Hansard of 1951, said this:
I have never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not begin by asking for more than his share of anything.
That of course was said by our distinguished friend-himself a major general

the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.
Thus, all too often, not only the size of the total allocation for defence but its distribution among the armed services depended more on the bargaining between the heads of the three services than on anything else. With today's developments, the dangers of this kind of uncritical, unquestioning acceptance of defence requirements is more dangerous than ever.
The London Economist had something to say about this matter concerning the British estimates when they were introduced into the house. I am quoting from the London Economist of February 20 of this year. It said this:
The danger is frankly that, while the backroom planners are busy working out the strategy of the new look, the authorities that really matter may succumb to the temptation, in this period of uncertainty, merely to pass round the money among the different claimants in very much the same proportions as they have been allowed to enjoy in the past; and then to leave each claimant to decide how he will spend that money in the new circumstances now emerging.
There are two reasons for fearing-the layman can, of course, never be sure that this may have liapoened in the estimates for 1954-55. In the first place, not only is the total defence estimate remarkably similar to the estimate for 1953-54; the different components are suspiciously similar too.
How well that applies to these estimates that are now before the house. There is a similarity to the components of a year ago before the explosion of a hydrogen bomb.
That this has been true in other countries is borne out by numerous articles that have appeared in the press of the world, articles by people who have made a study of defence and military affairs and who may be regarded as authorities. Walter Lippmann, I suppose, is regarded as one of the outstanding commentators on military affairs in the world at the present time. In his column of January 8 of this year he criticized the Truman administration and its attitude to some of these matters. He had this to say:
To put it bluntly, but I believe truly, the Truman administration lost control in the constitutional and meaningful sense of that word over the war-making powers of the United States. It lost control over the size and the character of the military establishment, over the high strategic planning in which statesmen, not soldiers, must have the last word, and over the theatre commanders abroad.
Supply-National Defence The visible consequences of all this were, for one thing, a gigantic military expansion which became all the more gigantic because it was regulated not by a lucid strategic policy but by the pressure of the military bureaucracies of the three services. Another consequence of the loss of control over the military power was the irreparable political errors of the Korean campaign, particularly the failure to halt at the 38th parallel, or at least at the waist of Korea, before the Chinese intervened.
Leaving out the reference to Korea, how can we in this parliament exercise our constitutional obligations with regard to this department? None of us knows what the requirements really are. None of us knows just how this money is really spent. I say to the house and to the minister that, although I have never been in favour of the proposal made from time to time that a royal commission, an outside body, should inquire into the Department of National Defence, I think we could appoint a competent committee of this house which could go into the affairs of the Department of National Defence and bring back to the house an assurance if it should prove to be so that the money is being well spent, that we are getting what we are paying for in this department.
At the moment there is not one of us who can say whether this estimate is right or wrong. There is not one of us who can say with certainty that the amount is adequate or that the amount is excessive. I think, and I hope to show in a moment, that if the matter is looked into in all probability it will be found that the amount is excessive and, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich suggested and as I suggested in the address, that it could be cut by at least 10 per cent. I believe it probably could be cut by more than 10 per cent if the matter were investigated thoroughly by the house.
To put it bluntly, we believe these estimates indicate that parliament has lost control of the Department of National Defence, and we believe that a thorough and careful investigation of the estimates now before the house should be made by the house or by a committee of the house before they are approved at this session of parliament. As I said a moment ago, I do not care to hazard a guess as to what savings could be made or the amount by which these estimates could be cut. As I pointed out in a former debate, the United States is reducing its appropriations by about 10 per cent and the United Kingdom by a lesser amount, and I believe that Canada could make a similar reduction in the defence appropriation.
I believe a thorough investigation of these estimates would confirm this view, and I want
4920	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence to cite some oi the details which to my mind help to confirm the statement I have just made. Of primary importance of course is that we shall be prepared to implement any undertakings made by this country under the charter of the United Nations, under the North Atlantic treaty or under other agreements that we have made or may make for collective security. In common with other western democracies, our defence program should no longer be geared, as the minister said today, to what has been termed "the crash objectives" of 1950 when war might have been imminent, but rather to what has been called this afternoon the long haul of future defence and peace or the long pull, whatever you care to call it.
I should like to remark right here and now that the North Atlantic treaty is more than a military alliance. It is more than a method of giving obsolete equipment to some of our allies, but as yet we have not begun to fulfil article 2 of the treaty. I want to say quite plainly and frankly that we of this party supported the North Atlantic treaty because we had the assurance that article 2 would be regarded as of fundamental importance. However, virtually nothing has been done to assist the economies of these countries. We have emphasized wholly and solely the military end of the agreement, and that is not good enough when we are fighting a cold war against a communist aggressor who uses economic distress as his principal vehicle of propaganda. It is time that we paid some attention to article 2 of the treaty for our mutual aid and prosperity.
A study of the United States and United Kingdom estimates for defence indicates that those countries have been moving quite rapidly into the new defensive position necessitated by considerations of the long haul while Canada's armed forces are still geared to the weapons and tactics of world war II. I have a number of quotations here from their estimates, statements and white papers which I could quote this afternoon, but I do not intend to do so because I have already quoted sufficiently.
As I said earlier, I am not suggesting that the new and terrible weapons of war make armies and navies unnecessary. Certainly they do not make the air force unnecessary. Quite the contrary, but I am suggesting that we could effect savings by reducing the stockpiling of weapons, planes and equipment which are either obsolete now or are certain to become obsolete in a comparatively short time. We do not know what stockpiling there has been, but if the figures in the previous estimates indicate the purchases that have been fMr. Coldwell.l

made there must be considerable stockpiling by the Department of National Defence.
It seems to us too that there is one branch of the Department of National Defence that is well worth supporting and even expanding. The field of electronics was referred to this afternoon and yet there is a reduction in the estimates for that branch of research, research carried on through the national research council and through our own defence research board. During world war II those organizations gave very significant aid in the achievement of victory. I agree immediately that such research should be undertaken by co-operation with those who will co-operate with us. That means to a very large extent, and in some fields almost exclusively, the United Kingdom and other members of the commonwealth. This should be done so that research efforts can be coordinated and duplication and waste among us avoided and, indeed, because we do cooperate, the program can be speeded up.
As an example, I mentioned a little earlier and I might mention again what might be done in this field. Instead of Canada embarking at great expense upon the production or experimentation of certain new types of planes, we could I think co-operate with Britain more fully. It is generally admitted that Britain leads the world in the development and production of aircraft. Why should we go to the expense of building and equipping new plants, designing new planes when we could co-operate with Britain and together work out the designs for planes, thus saving us both a great deal of expense?
Then, it seems to us that reconsideration should be given to the proposals for defence construction for all three services. We are told that this program of construction, building and so on across the country has now passed its peak. Apparently a further wave of expenditures in this field is foreshadowed in the estimates. I feel the department should be called upon to justify those expenditures. So far as housing for our married men is concerned, yes; but after all that is only a comparatively small part of the appropriation. The need for the other facilities should be carefully examined by this house before the appropriations are approved. If they were scrutinized I believe reductions could be made in that field.
I suggest that to continue to stockpile weapons and ammunition on a large scale, at a time when revolutionary changes are being made in weapons and armaments generally, is nothing but the greatest wastefulness. Apparently, expenditures for such weapons and ammunition as may become obsolete are

to continue on a fairly large scale under these estimates. I feel that should be reviewed by this house or by a committee of this house. Then we have noted, too, that the United States is contemplating a reduction of its armed forces in Korea. We maintain a brigade in Korea, and if the United States can withdraw some forces why could we not bring back at least a battalion? The maintenance of troops in Korea is a costly undertaking because we ship supplies not only by sea but by air. While we do that with some of our own military transport planes, we also hire planes from a private company, the Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
It seems to us that if the United States can withdraw some of her troops from Korea, we could withdraw some also. It might be possible to place in reserve some of our ships, our cruisers for example. They are costly to maintain at sea, and they are costly to maintain in port. I have noticed the whole emphasis in the United States and in the United Kingdom, so far as their navies are concerned, is to get away from battleships and cruisers in favour of anti-submarine vessels and aircraft carriers. I saw the other day that the United Kingdom has suspended building activities on three new cruisers, the Tiger, the Defence, and the Blake.
Then, as the minister has already said, we have a large air force in Europe. I believe there are 12 fighter squadrons there. Until recently there were few such squadrons in Canada. We were almost defenceless in the air. I want to say to the minister that no other country had denuded itself of air protection for the common effort as completely as Canada did. The minister told us it costs over $600 million a year to equip, transport and maintain an R.C.A.F. division in Europe. Even if we returned six of those fighter squadrons to Canada a substantial saving would be made, and there would be at least a more efficient fighter protection in Canada if that were required. Certainly no one could accuse us of not contributing equitably to the NATO effort if we did that.
We should review carefully Canada's expenditure for aircraft, which is given on pages 44 and 45 of the white paper. The estimate for 1954-55 is for $430 million, and that represents 43-5 per cent of our air force expenditures. This is a far greater proportion of the expenditure for aircraft than the proportion I noticed in the United Kingdom estimate, which I believe is in the order of 29 per cent or 30 per cent. Other items of the estimates that require scrutiny are numerous, but I am going to give only a few examples. In the details we are told that 83276-312
Supply-National Defence we have 1,000 inspectors of stores, in addition to the inspection staffs of each of the services. These 1,000 inspectors cost $3,500,000. I am not going to deny that adequate inspection is necessary, but the present estimates provide for no less than $12-5 million for all the inspection services compared with only $10-5 million at the height of our war effort, 194344. How could that be justified? Perhaps the minister can justify it when he speaks.
Even the Currie report of the investigation into the forces did not indicate losses as high as the cost of these inspection services. These and other savings run into many tens of millions of dollars when you add them all up. I did a little arithmetic the other day and was amazed at the total I got. I am not going to name it because some of my figures were the result of looking into the estimates and endeavouring to estimate what the totals would be. I am not going to do that at the moment; but, when we have heard from the minister further and we have gone into these estimates further, we may come to a conclusion as to just what savings could be effected in this department. I say tens of millions of dollars but I believe the savings would run into hundreds of millions of dollars -not many hundreds, but hundreds of millions of dollars. Please do not misunderstand and think I am making a plea for a reduction in income tax as a result of defence savings; not at all.
As I said, I should like to see more emphasis on article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, mutual economic aid, which would be perhaps costly to us. I should like to see Canada take more of a leading part in urging and providing technical aid for the underprivileged nations of the world. I know that is limited by the facilities of the technical aid organization, the Colombo plan facilities and so on, but we could do more than we are doing now, so some of those funds could be used for that. If we improved the living standards of these underprivileged parts we would be doing much to make inoperative the propaganda of totalitarian agitators, whether they are of the fascist or of the communist variety. We have sometimes overlooked the fact that the danger of totalitarianism does not come only from communism but comes equally through various forms of fascism across the world.
Then some of the savings could be used effectively in Canada. We could use them for our social services, in part for a national health plan, for improving the amenities of life in this country. I have always been a very warm advocate of doing something for the cultural life of Canada. I like to see

Supply-National Defence the national gallery buying a few pictures; I like to see the suggestion made that we should encourage a national drama, a national opera, national ballet, national music in the form of symphonies, and the like.
But, first of all, of course, we should see that we have those facilities in the social services for health and well-being as well as the cultural things. The hon. member spoke about aircraft carriers, and that has reminded me that the other day I read we were going to replace the Magnificent with the Bonaventure-in fact, we were told this in the house-and that the Bonaventure would operate off the east coast.
What are we going to do with the Magnificent? Here I am suggesting an expenditure of money.	Why not remodel and
modernize the Magnificent and make her suitable for what the hon. member suggested, namely the carrying of helicopters-indeed, why not redesign the Bonaventure to do the same thing? Why not use one of them on the east coast and the other on the west- because if aggression should come we cannot be sure that it will come on the east coast; neither are we sure that it will not come on the west. It would be well if we had an additional ship-and this of course would entail additional expenditure. However, that is the kind of expenditure of which I am sure the House of Commons would approve, because hon. members would understand the purpose of it.
From reports that have been made, I do not know to what extent Canada's forces are receiving adequate training for atomic warfare, if such should come. I do not know what they have learned about the use of atomic weapons, guided missiles and the like. Are our forces being trained as are the armed forces in other countries? It does not mean that they have to use those weapons, but they could use weapons simulated to meet training requirements. Is this being done?
If my information is correct the Canadian army has not yet been given training in airborne operations at the brigade level. So far that has not been done, according to my information. Yet we hear a great deal about the necessity for having airborne troops. Of course, in our country air defence and the ability to cope with a group of enemy soldiers parachuted into northern Canada is of primary and fundamental importance. Our forces may have to be flown quite a distance to fulfil this task, and might be required in brigade strength.
I am told, too, by military men that much of the army training is obsolete, and that in this respect to a great extent the money
[Mr. Coldwell.1
is wasted. But whether that is true or not, I think emphasis should be placed on research; and as I said earlier, in that field all the co-operation possible should be undertaken with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries. And if the United States wishes to co-operate with us, well and good; we would be prepared to cooperate with them. If this co-operation were complete, as it should be, we believe it might effect very substantial savings in our estimates.
As I have said, these savings should be diverted into channels which would be beneficial to the world and to ourselves. Our plea is for a reconsideration of the estimates that have been presented to us, in the light of recent developments. And should this be done thoroughly we believe very substantial reductions can be made in the total estimates of the department, without impairing its efficiency and without jeopardizing the security of our country.
I am not going to discuss the problem of civil defence in relation to new weapons. That will come under another heading. Suffice it to say that we are now told by experts in the United States in this field that only the mass evacuation of populations of our larger centres would suffice in the event of raids bringing hydrogen bombs. What a prospect the world faces, if that is so! And I fear that it is so.
The minister told us that our radar defences are 90 per cent complete and in operation. Well, it is good to know that, but in collaboration with our radar defences we should have adequate fighting air and ground forces in this country. I have noted that recently some CF-lOO's have been located and are being used in Canada. But, as I said earlier, until very recently we had denuded ourselves of air defence through our contributions to NATO. I am not complaining about contributions to NATO; but I think we also have to think about our own defences, as well as the defences of western Europe, in the event of war.
I do not wish to say anything further, except to express the hope that the House of Commons will examine these estimates. It is true that in the main estimates information is given in great detail, and that they are set out very carefully indeed. I hope hon. members will see to it that, so far as we are able to bring it about, any wastes will be eliminated. But I think most of all we require, first, a thorough investigation into the activities of the department, and its estimates, by a committee of the House of Commons.

All of us are anxious to give our support to any necessary defensive plans for our own country, and to assist those who expect us to give assistance through the United Nations, NATO and the like. But the difficulty in which most of us find ourselves-and I fancy this includes hon. members on the government side as well as in the opposition-is that this department is a law unto itself. And because of the secret nature of many of its operations it is protected against thorough inquiry by the elected representatives of the people.
The age-old struggle in the British democracies has been to make certain that the civilian arm of government can and does control the military. And upon my soul, I think at the present time this House of Commons has very largely lost control of the defence department and the military arm of the nation; and I think we should do everything we can to restore a control that is properly the function of this parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the minister gave us a comprehensive survey of Canada's position, so far as our armed forces are concerned. He went into some detail in regard to the international situation, the military aspect of NATO, and some other matters. As a matter of fact his speech was so comprehensive and detailed that it was almost impossible for one to absorb all he said merely by listening. But I would make a suggestion to the minister. I do not know what he will think of it, but it would certainly simplify matters for those who have to speak immediately after him if it could be arranged in the future that he give his statement, and then allow the item to stand and continue the debate the next day or the day after in order to give hon. members an opportunity to study his statement in detail before speaking.
At the outset I should like to pay tribute to the members of the armed forces. These men of all the services have built themselves an enviable reputation wherever they have gone. They have served with distinction in every theatre of war where they have been called to act. Certainly, they have become well known for their courage, ability and resourcefulness in the field. More than that, the members of the Canadian armed forces have been well liked everywhere they have gone in other than official capacities. In other words, practically without exception they behave like gentlemen, regardless of where they are serving.
On many occasions, Mr. Chairman, we have been critical, and sometimes extremely critical, but that criticism has never applied to the members of the armed forces. We
83276-312^
Supply-National Defence have criticized the department for some of the policies they have brought down, and undoubtedly we shall continue to do so. But our criticisms have always been against the department, against the government and never against the armed forces or any of the individuals of the forces.
The situation in the world today, as the minister indicated, is extremely serious. I go along with the minister and hope also that in the future we shall not find ourselves embroiled in another all-out war. But we cannot allow ourselves to become too complacent. Things look bad. As a matter of fact, I picked up today's Journal and on the front page I saw the headline:	"Geneva
looks hopeless." I do not know what the article contains because I have not had an opportunity to read it.
With things stacking up the way they are, in every effort that has been made to bring the two opposing sides together, we cannot afford to relax our vigilance even for a moment. We are not actually engaged in a hot war at the present time, but we are in a war. It is not war as wars have been known down through the ages, which were brought about by trade wars and so on. It is a battle between two ways of life, between communism and democracy and between freedom and slavery. We must never forget that the forces of international communism, have no regard for life, or the individual;, they have no regard for promises made and they have no regard for any treaties that they may have signed. They are vicious. We must never forget also that world domination is their ultimate aim. They have made that known all through the years from the time of Marx and Engels right down to the present regime. I hope, and I know every hon. member hopes, that the peace overtures they are making at the present time and have been making recently are sincere. It is possible that the new administration in Russia has had a change of heart, but I would not bank on it too much. In other words, we have to take every opportunity afforded to maintain peace, but at the same time we must always be prepared for the worst.
We in this group have always supported defence spending. We feel that as long as a large defence program is necessary we should keep at it, and I can assure the minister he will have our wholehearted support in every expenditure that we feel is necessary for the carrying on of our defence program. We realize that with the situation the way it is today defence is all-important. We have been critical many times, not because the government is spending money, but of

Supply-National Defence how they are spending it. We have often maintained, as speakers who preceded me said today, there is no economy in the Department of National Defence. As a matter of fact, I have not found it in any department of government. The aims of the department undoubtedly are very high and to be commended, namely, the protection of our country. But sometimes the results leave a great deal to be desired. I cannot believe, Mr. Chairman, that we are getting a dollar value out of every dollar spent on defence. I think we discovered quite a bit in our defence expenditure committee last year, and in a small way the Currie report proved that there is waste and extravagance in the Department of National Defence.
I regret very much that the government did not see fit to set up the defence expenditure committee during this session. After all, we touched only the surface of defence spending during the last session. We covered a great deal of the ground as far as construction is concerned, but we did not get into the production of aircraft, arms or ammunition, or any of the things that we should like to have made a complete investigation into. I only hope-and I would ask the minister to discuss it with his colleagues-that a committee will be set up again next year, as early as possible in the session, and that it will be allowed to dig into the entire regime of defence spending.
May I say a brief word on fires at some of the installations? The minister made a statement in the house the other day in which he said that compared with civilian fires the percentage of damage was very low. I realize that, and well it should be, because in no other place do they have the facilities for sentries or fire protection and so on concentrated in such a small area. It is hard to believe that if the sentries are being posted as they should be a large blaze could develop before it was discovered. I realize that it could probably happen in some instances, but I cannot see how for example at the air station at Penhold, with the number of personnel there, a fire could get a good start and destroy a hangar, when one takes into consideration the facilities and the personnel there, particularly since they have sentries posted at all the hangars to see that such a thing does not happen.
The minister went to great length this afternoon to show how NATO had been built up to strength, not sufficient to defeat the communists, but strong enough to hold the line until the air power and the atomic power of the NATO countries could be used to interrupt any attack that might be made. I do not think they have the minimum that


the minister mentioned this afternoon. The aim for NATO as it was set down was for 90 divisions by 1954, or something like
1.350.000	men.
Perhaps the minister told us this afternoon the extent of the manpower within NATO forces at the present time, but if so I missed it and in any event I do not think it will amount to the figure I have mentioned. At any rate, the estimated power of the Russian forces alone, and in this connection I am taking the figures given by General Gruen-ther two years ago, amounted to 175 divisions, or something like 4 million men. That takes no account of the satellite forces, and they can certainly muster a great many more men in a hurry. In view of that, it is difficult to see how the NATO forces could hold the communist hordes for even a short time.
I have mentioned the Russian figures relative to about two years ago, and I would like the minister to bring us up to date on the estimated force the communists have at their command at the present time. I would like to know how much they have at their command in terms of land, air, and sea forces. In regard to their air power I would like to have some sort of resume as to the number of first-line bombers, light bombers, heavy bombers, and fighter planes they have at their disposal. As regards their naval power I would like to have a resume of the estimated number of first-line submarines, battleships and so on up the line. I do not know whether the minister has these figures, but I have no doubt he has some knowledge.
I paid particular attention to the minister's statement this afternoon to the effect that it was only as long as the NATO nations could maintain their productive superiority that we could hope to deter the communists from attack. I am not sure that we have that productive superiority.
Speaking on the defence estimates in April 1952 I quoted from a technical and trade magazine called Aviation Age giving some figures of Russian productive capacity as far as the air power is concerned, though that was two years ago. That magazine estimated that Russia had about 85 aircraft factories, more than 28 engine plants, and produced something in the neighbourhood of
22.000	aircraft during the past year. That, of course, would be in 1951. Perhaps I should quote briefly from my speech at that time as reported at page 1100 of Hansard for April 3, 1952:
I should like to refer briefly to six points which were dealt with in that magazine under dateline. Washington, March 13. The first is that there are about 15 large. 30 medium, and 40 smaller plants producing airframes within Russia.

That is in addition to the engine plants and aircraft factories I mentioned a moment ago. The quotation continues:
The Russian ministry for the aircraft industry supervises 360 factories which do all or most of their work for the red air force. Then they have a number of contributing industries such as 20 rubber factories and 15 to 18 aluminum plants.
The magazine goes on to mention that each plant is capable of producing something like 3,600 engines; and, except for the fact that there is a bottleneck in the aluminum industry, the output could be raised to 50,000 or
60,000	Russian planes per year.
It was pointed out that during the same period the United States had 27 airframe factories, about 15 smaller ones, and some 30 other companies building major subsections, etc. In that speech I added:
To get back to the claimed production of 22,000 aircraft for Russia, it is believed that about 10,700 are fighting planes, 539 reconnaissance planes, 3,060 light and medium bombers, 1,246 heavy bombers, 1,430 transport planes and 5,000 trainer and liaison planes. The production last year in the United States was something like 5,000 planes.
Now, I do not know how authentic these figures are, but the magazine Aviation Age is considered a pretty reliable sort of publication, and the figures given would indicate that our productive capacity, at least as applied to aircraft, is far below that of the Russians, at least in 1951-52. I hope the minister can assure us that we are now far ahead of them in production in the NATO countries.
The minister indicated this afternoon that we have very few targets in Canada which would attract-but before going on with that, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should call it six o'clock.
