speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess at six o'clock I was about to say that this afternoon the minister indicated that there were in Canada few targets that would rate an attack by aircraft carrying either the atomic or the hydrogen bomb. In that statement I can agree wholeheartedly with the minister. There are in Canada very few centres that are highly industrialized and that would therefore make a good target. But that very fact brings to mind the question we
Supply-National Defence have raised many times in this chamber-
I know I have raised it on many occasions- namely that of decentralization.
The minister knows that if about half a dozen of the cities in Canada were to be wiped out by a hydrogen bomb attack, our industrial potential would be practically wiped out. He knows that it would take very few bombs to absolutely ruin our production. We in this group particularly, as well as many of the other members, have constantly asked the government to put more and more essential war production centres in the prairie provinces, inland somewhere in British Columbia or in the maritimes, so that even if the larger centres here in Canada might be bombed we would still have sufficient productive capacity to carry on.
That suggestion brings to our minds another consideration, namely that of transportation. If the larger railway centres in this country were put out of action, our entire transportation system would be at a standstill. As the situation is at present, if a concerted attack were made on any part of this country outside of the highly populated areas, we have not the facilities by means of which to carry to the field of action the necessary men, materials, armaments and so on. I know that in a statement not long ago the minister said that we in Canada were not in too much danger of a concentrated attack, that any attack on this country would be spotty and of a minor nature, and would probably be made by paratroopers or something like that. However, we cannot allow ourselves to become complacent. We do not know what is going to happen. If the communists should decide to make an attack on the United States rather than on some other part of the world, Canada would be the logical jumping-off place. We cannot allow ourselves to get the "It Can't Happen Here" complex.
In order to facilitate the transportation of ground troops, materials and so on that cannot be carried by air, I think we need an adequate highway system throughout this country. I can think of one good instance, and it is one that has been mentioned in this chamber many times. If an attack should be made somewhere in the north central part of British Columbia or at least if there should happen to be a concentration of troops there, we have no way whatsoever of transporting materials and men through the Yellowhead pass and into British Columbia. I use that as an example because, in my opinion, that route is absolutely necessary. In view of that necessity, I think the government should take greater action and should co-operate more fully with the provinces in setting up
4926	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence not a trans-Canada highway but a trans-Canada highway system that will be adequate.
When I came back to Ottawa after the Easter recess, I was on the train with a considerable number of service personnel coming back from Korea and I had a rather interesting talk with some of them during the train trip. I asked one sergeant what was lacking in Korea as far as the Canadian soldiers were concerned or what they needed most in Korea that they did not have. I was rather surprised at his answer. What he said was this:	We have good equipment; we are
-among the best equipped men in the field in Korea. Our food is good. We cannot complain on those grounds. The medical equipment is good. The dental equipment is good. But what we need in Korea more than anything else are some service canteens.
I know that we went into that matter about three years ago and that the minister claimed there was no necessity for them. I know that on that occasion 1 protested quite strongly as did other members of the opposition and some members on the government side. The sergeant to whom I was talking said they lacked that little touch of Canada while away from home. They obtained ail their canteen supplies and so on through NAAFI.
I do not think I need to say too much about NAAFI. The returned men here all know of the complaints-at least I do-that we all had against NAAFI during the second war. For one thing, they rely a great deal on the profits they can get. The men could not get their Canadian cigarettes, chocolate bars and so on. The tea was undrinkable and the coffee was worse. But even of more importance, it was a fact that the men could not walk into a canteen and be greeted by Canadians. The man to whom I was speaking said that the recreation facilities in the matter of canteens and so on were the greatest lack as far as operations in Korea were concerned.
I would therefore urge the minister to reconsider the stand he took at that time and to allow these various service clubs to go into Korea in the same way as they travelled all over the world with the boys during the last two wars.
In my conversation with the boys I also found out something else that was rather interesting. It had to do with the accommodation in Korea, particularly around the brigade headquarters. During all of the campaign the boys had been billeted in tents, but by sheer coincidence a few days before the Prime Minister's visit the tents suddenly disappeared and a profusion of quonset huts came on the scene. There was no shortage of them but they had not been able to get them for three years prior to that. For


example, after the radio station had appeared to be at a standstill for quite some time it suddenly went on the air just three days before the Prime Minister arrived. At about the same time sudden, feverish activity with respect to the large recreational centre resulted in quite a definite change taking place a few days prior to the Prime Minister's visit.
After the minister and others have visited some of the overseas bases of the Canadian forces they return with glowing tales, but such things as I have mentioned make us wonder whether or not these stories are perhaps a little rosier than the situation is in reality. I urge the minister once more, as I have done on other occasions, that when he or his parliamentary assistant or other officials make their tours of the Canadian overseas establishments they should take at least one or two of the opposition members with them. If things are as good over there as the minister says they are, then he should be only too glad to have opposition members come back here, stand up in the house and say how good things are. On the other hand, if things are not as good as he says, then it is time that the Canadian people found out.
I have a couple of other brief references. I notice that the minister makes reference on page 11 of the white paper to the fact that nuclear information is being distributed among the NATO forces to enable them to take full advantage of these weapons. I should like the minister to elaborate on that slightly and tell us the extent of that information. I should like to know whether it is merely information as to the method of detonating the bombs or whether it goes a little further and gives information as to the set-up, the means of production and so forth.
To come to the navy, I note that the minister has indicated in the white paper that within a few months of the outbreak of hostilities the Canadian navy would have a hundred ships in action. I should like to know how many of these ships could be considered first-line ships, how many could be used for convoy or escort duty in the Atlantic or Pacific, how many could be used as coastal escort vessels and how many would have to be sunk to form barriers to keep the enemy from getting into our bays. He also said that there were 58 ships in commission at the present time. I should like to know how many of the 58 can be considered first-line ships. I should like to know whether or not they are capable of carrying out anti-submarine warfare as it is known today or whether they are the old, cumbersome, corvette-type escort vessel that was obsolete before the end of the last war.

The Canadian navy has always been engaged primarily in escort work, and once again I should like to ask the minister to give serious consideration to the production of small aircraft carriers, possibly a modernized version of the merchant aircraft carriers of the last war, a ship that is not too fast but will carry a small reconnaissance plane that can search the area immediately around the convoy in order to discover the presence of enemy submarines. In my opinion the aircraft launched from the small converted merchant aircraft carriers won the battle of the Atlantic for us. The cost is not great. They are not an expensive ship, and so far as escort work is concerned they are worth their weight in gold.
The minister referred to the air defence plan, the radar screen and so on. Like the minister, I visited one of the radar stations in the screen some time ago, and I too witnessed the interception of so-called enemy planes by fighter aircraft. I was impressed this afternoon by the figure given as to the high percentage of kills made in the air exercises. But I am wondering just how effective the air defence plan would be against highly modern, fast, high-altitude bombers. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, no matter how efficient the radar screen may be it cannot do us any good if the air power behind the screen is insufficient. We have to have enough modern, well-equipped aircraft here in Canada in order to back up that screen. As the minister says, with the type of aerial bomb being constructed today, not many aircraft would have to get through the screen to wreck absolutely a good many of the larger cities of Canada.
As I mentioned at the outset, we in this group will continue to support any necessary defence expenditures or defence effort. The only stipulation we put on our support is that we get value for our dollars, that for every cent that goes into our defence effort we get a cent's worth of value in return. We can only hope that by negotiations or some other means the international crisis will be solved before too long and people will know once more what peace and security are.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we listened with interest this afternoon to the minister's review of world conditions. I thought it was a typical statement by the minister, a general review with a touch of the external affairs debate in it; some comment about the amount of money that Canada is expending on preparations for defensive purposes; some comment on the navy; slightly more extensive comment on the air force; some mention of
Supply-National Defence the army, but no close attention to the question of detail. The minister started off by suggesting that a clear meaning should be given to some of the expressions that have been used recently in international affairs, such as "massive retaliation", "the new look", and "the long haul". I had hoped he would have taken my advice on an earlier occasion and dropped the use of the word "aggression", and used instead the simple word "war". It has a very clear and well understood meaning. However, he has not come around to that yet.
I agree with the minister that the development of nuclear weapons affords a great deterrent to a major war, but that there is no evidence yet before us that small wars will not occur, that is, the wars of limited objective. For that reason we still have to place reliance on the so-called conventional weapons. To the extent that the minister and his department are maintaining our forces along conventional lines, I think that they are right. We have not yet reached, as he stated, the push-button warfare stage. However, I thought that there was a weakness in the minister's statement. I thought it was more a quartermaster general's review of the situation, mentioning supplies, accommodation, equipment and things of that nature, with a little word from the adjutant general's branch concerning personnel. We did not hear much, if anything, from the point of view of the general staff, those who are responsible for strategy and tactics. I had hoped the minister would apply his mind to the fighting effectiveness of our armed services.
I think that over the years his attitude has become the infrastructure approach to the problems. He likes to tell us about the camps, the accommodation and so on, for the forces. I have no objection to seeing the services properly housed. I believe that is a good thing. It is good for morale and it is good for health. There is no reason why they should not be well looked after. It is the question of emphasis about which I express some surprise. For example, the minister gave us one of those typical sentences of his in respect of our service people in Europe. He told us that they had the finest living accommodation for the men, their wives and children anywhere in the world. Well, that is interesting and we are glad to hear that they are being well looked after.
But I do not think that strikes at the root of the problem in respect of defence. My interest is, what are we getting for our defence dollar in fighting effectiveness? To that question, over the last two or three
4928	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence years, no satisfactory answer has been forthcoming. The minister said nothing or next to nothing concerning weapons and ammunition; nothing about artillery or tanks and very little about rockets or new weapons. He did not even make any statement or announcement to us about the possibility of the Canadian army adopting a new rifle. Perhaps that will come later when we get to the second item of these estimates. I thought it was of sufficient importance for an announcement to be made during the course of the minister's major speech. On this subject he said nothing about the need for increased mobility of our forces, and that is a matter of considerable concern to those who are in charge of the NATO forces in Europe.
I thought the minister might have gone a little further into the problem of what warfare might be like in the future in this atomic age; that he might have pointed out to us that atomic weapons might be used on the battlefield as between two opposing armies; that they would cause a greater area of destruction; that they would prevent the massing of troops in a leisurely way as has been done in other wars; that heavily populated seaports and vast assembly areas would constitute a grave hazard with atomic weapons available. I thought he would go on to point out that under circumstances such as those, the need to assemble forces rapidly to launch an assault and to disperse them rapidly in case of an enemy attack with atomic artillery would require greater mobility than our army possesses today.
We do not want to be prepared merely for the last war or the one that preceded that. We have to keep in mind that other changes are in the air. It would have been very useful to the house to have had some statement from the minister along those lines.
I admit that it enters the realm of tactics, perhaps of strategy, but it is only if we understand what we are up against that we can give full accord to the plans of the minister for his preparations. It is only then that the people of Canada would continue unanimously to provide the money necessary for the equipment and expansion of our forces. We surely must know how they are going to be used, and what our plans are with regard to future developments in warfare.
If we are going to have mobility for our army, tracked vehicles for cross country movement are essential and air transport for troops and supplies is essential. The use of the helicopter is a development that is proceeding apace with some armies in other parts of the world. Surely the minister


might have dwelt upon this subject, and shown us whether or not our army was up to date in its planning and in its training. In a recent interview with the press, General Montgomery said that the requirement for the troops under his command was mobility and more mobility. What are we doing about that? I shall refer to that a little later.
I want now to just touch on the minister's speech of last November, to which he referred two or three times. I recall, and Hansard records, that last November the minister entered the debate on the speech from the throne and expressed surprise that nobody had mentioned the subject of defence. I shall just quote his words as reported at page 358 of Hansard for November 26. He said:
Mr. Speaker, this debate opened two weeks ago today, and a most extraordinary thing has happened which X must confess surprises me very much, that is that during this whole period the subject of defence has not so far been mentioned.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and myself undertook to deal with the subject later on in that debate, in answer to this challenge of the minister. Of course there was no opportunity for him to reply at that stage, and he has not taken the opportunity now to answer some of the questions we raised on that occasion.
I was suggesting to him that it would be a fine thing if the Minister of National Defence were to interest himself in the development of the armoured corps, and in the development of an armoured personnel carrier for infantry, in order that the lives of our Canadian soldiers might be saved, in the event of their being engaged in battle under conditions such as occurred during the last war in northwestern Europe. I had hoped the minister would say something about that today, although some interval has elapsed since I posed the questions to him.
I asked him this:	Why is the Canadian
army as a whole not being brought up to the standards required in modern warfare? Why is the armoured corps not being enlarged and returned to strength and, most important of all, why is not armoured protection for our infantry being provided?
To the last question I find what is perhaps a partial answer as it is set out at page 39 of the white paper. Paragraph 147 says:
The army is also developing a new tracked carrier for the infantry.
I think the sentence, however, is rather carelessly written. The word "carrier" has been used in the past to refer, not to a troop-carrying vehicle but to a machine-guncarrying vehicle. It will be recalled that we had Bren gun carriers in the second

world war. Who is to tell what this is? If it is to be an armoured personnel carrier, or a troop carrying vehicle, why not say so? But simply to say that a new tracked carrier for the infantry is being provided is not clear enough.
However, I will assume that the minister and his advisers have now come around to the view that the vehicle which was so effective in the second world war in the saving of lives of Canadian soldiers is now going to be used in the present Canadian army, and incorporated in their training. It will be a major step forward if that is done; and I will simply assume that that is now part of the policy of the department.
During the course of my remarks last November, and on other occasions, I have dealt with this topic. I have also dealt with the armoured corps and have lamented the position to which it has fallen within the Canadian army. I said it had become the Cinderella of the Canadian army.
Just a year ago, when I was discussing this matter, the minister said in reply, on April 16, 1953, as reported at page 3981 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre again referred to our playing down the armoured corps. There is no intention of doing that and there is no indication of that being done. Everyone appreciates the great importance of armour and its proper place in any fighting team.
Well, what has happened in the course of the year? If everyone appreciates that, and if the armoured corps is not being played down, then why is it not being enlarged? Why is it not being utilized effectively? I made considerable reference during the course of that speech in the house to how well the Canadian infantry corps, as well as the artillery and the engineers, had been trained, due to the campaign in Korea and to the stationing of troops in Europe, as well as to the rotation of units that had occurred. 1 dealt at some length with the number of senior officers in those corps of the army who had received training. There were certainly four infantry brigadiers, and a score or perhaps a dozen or more lieutenant colonels, and over a score of majors, and more than that, of company commanders and seconds in command-men who under actual service conditions received training in the command of those formations of troops. The result has been that the Canadian infantry corps, as well as the artillery and the engineers, under this process must have become a very effective fighting team.
But in the same interval what has happened to the armoured corps? This question may be of no importance, until one recalls
Supply-National Defence the status of the armoured corps in the second world war, when it constituted about half of the Canadian army-two armoured divisions, two tank brigades, and so on. But what have we now? Well, we are reduced to two regiments. What training have they received during the Korean war or while the brigade has been stationed in Europe? One squadron only is serving in Korea and one in Europe, and being rotated. The tanks of those squadrons are apparently being farmed out to the infantry regiment. Perhaps they operate now and again, or have operated as squadrons. But I doubt it in Korea. There has been no opportunity for a major in command of that squadron to exercise his squadron as a whole, and there has been no competent training for majors commanding squadrons in the armoured corps. There is no training for seconds in command of armoured regiments. There is no training for lieutenant colonels of armoured regiments. So that at the conclusion of this period during which the Canadian infantry corps as well as the engineers and artillery have become fully trained under conditions of warfare, the armoured corps has been only partially trained. And no plans have been announced to us at the present time indicating any extension of the training of the armoured corps.
The result is that the officers of this part of the army simply cannot be promoted. There is no expansion of their opportunity because there is nowhere for them to go. I do not know whether the present lieutenant colonels of the armoured regiments will become brigadiers in command of infantry brigades; I do not know that. But I think that those men who have had service as lieutenant colonels overseas would take precedence over those who have had experience only here in Canada, with a reduced force under their command.
I pointed out at that time that this is a bad thing for the Canadian army. It is out of balance in relation to the way in which armies are formed elsewhere. The British army, for instance, is not neglecting its armoured corps. I believe they have three armoured divisions in Europe. The Russians have not neglected their armoured strength, nor have the Americans. Why have the Canadians-and particularly when we were experts in the use of armour during the last war?
The minister mentioned economy in men and money as one of the essential points in the defence program. Well, I would point out to him that you have economy in the use of men when you use armoured vehicles. You can have a much greater fire power with several hundred fewer men by using
4930	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence an armoured brigade instead of an infantry brigade. And if they happen to be engaged in battle, you have a very much smaller casualty list. This has been proved time and again. I have advanced evidence before to this effect in the house.
In the face of these facts, why is the armoured corps in the Canadian army neglected? The minister rejected our proposal last year for the maintenance of an armoured brigade in Europe and an armoured brigade in Canada, with rotation between the two. If he will not accept that suggestion, then I put forward this. Why not constitute an armoured brigade here in Canada? Activate another regiment. Let us have three regiments and an armoured brigade headquarters, and train the personnel and the senior officers in the use of armour. It goes farther than just that.
Let me look for one moment at the training program of the Canadian army as I see it in the white paper and from reading the newspapers. The brigade in Europe participated in an exercise not so long ago and was pitted against a British armoured division, and of course acquitted itself nobly. It was a good exercise for the brigade commander and his subordinate commander, a good signal exercise, good for the transportation of the troops, for the supply of them in the field. It would be splendid for the men themselves participating in the open and simulating modern warfare, but quite unrealistic, of course. An infantry brigade versus an armoured division just would not survive under actual conditions unless it had superior artillery, because what effective fighting strength has an infantry battalion against an armoured regiment? They could put out mine fields, use a few bazookas, but under shellfire, under cover of darkness, they have no effective protection against tanks.
I notice on page 30 of the white paper we are informed in paragraph 115 that brigade groups will be assembled for collective training at Camp Wainwright and Camp Gage-town during the summer of 1954. It also says:
A signal exercise will be conducted by headquarters first Canadian infantry division at Camp Borden in 1954, in which the divisional headquarters, headquarters second and third Canadian infantry brigades, headquarters of supporting arms and services, and signals units will participate.
That is a typical signal exercise, where officers operate from vehicles or at desks, use the wireless and simulate attack and withdrawal and so on. There is no use of troops under those circumstances.


On page 7 of the white paper we find some mention of the mobile striking force consisting of an infantry battalion with airborne units of artillery, engineers, signals, army service corps and medicals. There is no suggestion there that they have been formed into a brigade, or that it has been exercised as a brigade, and there is no mention of armoured formations at all.
I was saying that this reaches farther than simply the provision of armour to balance the army. It reaches farther than that in this way. We must assume that if we are engaged in a war of limited objective, it might be in terrain where armoured forces could be used. We must assume that if we are engaged in a somewhat larger war, armoured forces will be used. The enemy have armoured forces. Therefore the point is that unless we train the high command in the Canadian army in the use of armour we shall be in a very serious position in a state of war.
I say that it is just nonsense to be preparing simply infantry forces-and we are talking about forming a division of infantry -unless we balance against that the necessary armour to give them protection and support. If we do not provide the armour for the Canadian army, we do not train the senior officers. If we do not train the senior officers, we face a serious situation in time of war. I stood in awe of senior officers for a large portion of my life; but with the passing of the years that awe has diminished very considerably. I have the greatest respect, of course, for my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, but he will agree with me it is essential for the high command, for divisional and corps commanders, to understand the use of all arms within the army. We had many experiences in the second world war of that where people unfamiliar with armoured formations were not able to use them effectively. Repeatedly I told men under my command when we were engaged in exercises in England at which they grumbled: "Put up with it; do anything that you are told to do under these conditions because we are training the high command, and you may live a bit longer if the high command gets trained."
I am a bit worried about the Canadian army. We have a great number of experienced senior officers still with us in the service, and all credit to them for staying in the service, and all honour to them. I respect them. A great many of them have active service experience and understand conditions, but a new crop of officers is being

produced, and I doubt whether that new crop of officers is being thoroughly trained. How can they be thoroughly trained unless the armoured corps is brought back to its position within the Canadian army that it occupied heretofore? It simply means that the experienced senior officers in the Canadian infantry corps, in the engineers and in the artillery, are going to rise to the top. They will become the major generals and lieutenant generals; they will command the divisions and the corps and they will not know very much about armour. No armoured corps officer is going to reach high position because no senior armoured corps officer is being fully trained at the present time. We have no armoured brigade; we have no armoured division, and there, Mr. Chairman, is a weakness in the Canadian army which I think should be corrected.
I had hoped that the minister would deal with some of these pressing problems instead of giving us just that quartermaster general's view of the situation. It is an effective fighting force that we want. We want to know how our defence dollar is being spent. Is it producing effective fighting forces? Are we producing with that defence dollar the means for protecting the lives of our men? They will fight gallantly under any conditions. They will die as gallantly as the defenders of Dien Bien Phu, if placed under similar circumstances, but that is not war; that is suicide. The Canadian soldier, who is a first-class soldier, if well trained, should never be subjected to conditions under which he is placed at a disadvantage. My hope is that the Canadian army will become the most effective fighting force available within the NATO countries, and that it will have the full equipment for modern conditions; that it will have the mobility that is required for modern warfare, and that it will have the trained staff that is required in order to utilize to its fullest effect artillery and armour, infantry and engineers and so on. Equipped with the best of weapons, equipped with track vehicles for cross-country purposes, equipped with those protective troop carrying vehicles for the infantry, and equipped with transport aeroplanes and helicopters, if those are found to be satisfactory for use in the field, equipped in this way, brought up to date, modernized, the Canadian army would be something of which we would be prouder than we are at the present time, although we are very proud of it. It would then be an effective fighting force and there would be protection for our men if they were ever placed under modern conditions of warfare, for they would be an integrated, coordinated force which would serve to train the high command, and if we were ever
Supply-National Defence called upon to undertake war in future we would achieve the success which has been granted to the Canadian soldiers in the field in other wars in which Canada has been engaged.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, coming into the chamber this evening I noticed that the committee on procedure was sitting. It struck me at that time, after listening to the Minister of National Defence making his comprehensive statement, then listening to the official spokesmen on defence matters for the Conservative party, our own chief spokesman and the member who spoke on behalf of the Social Credit party, that if this general debate on the defence estimates stopped right there, so far as general statements are concerned, it would be much better, and we could then go into the estimates in detail, thus saving a lot of time. To my surprise, when I was upstairs in the cafeteria, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is a member of that committee, pretty well expressed the same opinion, so we may be getting around to the time when we can avoid duplication in debate.
Listening to the Minister of National Defence this afternoon, one was struck by the fact that defence today is perhaps the biggest business in the world. The attention of the world is focused on the possibility of war, making preparations for war, and spending huge chunks of national income to that end. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar this afternoon dealt in detail with the defence program as set out in the white paper and I am going to try to avoid any duplication of his remarks. But, as I have already said, the thing that struck me was the difficulty of anyone in or out of the government estimating exactly what the cost of defence might be under the circumstances which today confront the world.
We are in that position simply because our program is defensive, and because we are on the defensive. The people against whom we are arming to defend ourselves are on the offensive, and they are in a position to choose their own battleground and time their attack, when it is going to be and where it will be, and there is no one either on that side of the house or on this in a position to say just when that attack will come. That is what makes the problem not only of estimating the cost but of criticizing the cost so very difficult, because the whole thing is merely a guess based on a hypothetical war. You cannot estimate that cost down to the last dollar, though you can probably make some good guesses.

Supply-National Defence
I could make a speech with a lot of words that would sound all right but which would perhaps not read quite so well, and after I had finished I would not have said anything. But what I am going to try to do is to pinpoint the two things which stand out in my mind in relation to the defence program, and I think they are pretty clear.
The first of these is Canada's defence objectives as set out on page 5 of the white paper, and I think we should keep these in mind. Anything we do in this chamber, particularly of a national or international character, should have a very clearly defined objective, and the first objective set out there very briefly states:
The objectives of our defence policy remain the same as heretofore:
(1)	The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
That is set down as our first objective, to see that this country is sufficiently prepared in the event of a direct attack to resist that attack. And then it goes on to say:
(2)	implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations.
And so on. That is our second objective. And again, in section 9, on the same page, prominence is again given to the first paragraph under those objectives, namely defence against direct attack. That should be the first consideration as far as Canada's national defence program is concerned, and that is the thing to which we, as members of the opposition, should be directing our attention in order to see that the objectives set out by the government are properly planned.
The minister this afternoon did not say anything about what in my judgment is one of the first requirements in any defence program, and that is that one of the first things we should do, if we expect the support of the people who pay taxes and thereby provide the wherewithal for this defence program, is to make it very clear to the general public, and particularly to service personnel, why we are arming ourselves, against whom we are arming to defend ourselves, and what we might expect in the future.
Hon. members will no doubt recall that Bill Boss wrote some very critical articles from Korea early in the Korean war and he said that as far as Canadian soldiers were concerned the thing they did not understand and which was never made clear to them was what they were fighting for. The minister neglected to deal with that particular side of the defence program.
However, I have an editorial in my hand which indicates that the defence department is working on that problem. This editorial states that at Acadia University and McGill


University in Montreal a series of lectures on that subject is being given which will eventually be put into book form to be distributed among service personnel. I think that is something which is badly needed because we cannot keep on telling the people of Canada, the United States, or any other country that a continuous war is necessary in order that they may live. We must not forget that we have had practically nothing but war during the lifetime of the present generation, and it must be made clear to them exactly why we are carrying on this huge defence program. I am glad to see the department is doing something about bringing that aspect of the situation to the attention of service personnel, and I think these matters should be more widely publicized so they will be brought to the attention of the average Canadian citizen.
The second thing about which I should like to say a few words is this question that has been referred to by practically all those who have spoken, namely that of the danger of an atomic war, of the throwing of the hydrogen bomb, the possibility of setting the world afire and all that kind of thing as related to our present defence program. As far as I am concerned, I am not afraid of the throwing of the atomic bomb or the hydrogen bomb. I do not think that there is anyone in Russia, the United States or Canada who does not realize that if either the hydrogen bomb or the atomic bomb is thrown, there is not going to be anything left. I do not think there is any country in this world today that wants to commit either national or international suicide. In the event of either Russia or the United States deciding to throw that bomb, all I can say is this. Planes will load up in Russia with bombs for the North American continent. We will load planes in the United States with bombs for Russia. Each group will arrive at their destination, will bomb their targets and return; and when they get back home there will be nothing to land on. Where do they go from there? The situation is as fantastic as that, without any doubt.
I do not think there is anyone today in any kind of a position of authority to give an order to begin that kind of action who is foolish enough to do so, because nobody can win. A great deal of that propaganda, of course, may be coming from certain sources for the purpose of mixing people up on this question of defence. I do not think any such order is going to be given or that any such action is going to take place. In my opinion we are in for a long siege of the kind of thing we are getting in Korea and Indochina. I believe we are going to get a great deal more of that kind of thing.

I am convinced-as I have been for a long time-that the objective of Russia today is to take control of Asia and that she is not going to do it with atomic bombs or hydrogen bombs. The pattern has already been set. With all due respect to everyone who has expressed the opinion that there is a danger of this other thing happening, I would suggest to them that with all of this talk of new weapons, the only practical demonstrations we have had during the past few years have been in Korea and Indo-China. In both of these actions, manpower was the decisive factor. In my judgment, for some considerable time to come the decisive factor will be manpower with ground weapons. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that we are not placing enough emphasis on armament. I am convinced that is the kind of thing for which we must be prepared for a long time to come.
This afternoon the Minister of National Defence said that the policy of the communist party in the matter of world domination has not been changed. I agree with him. It has not been changed. But they are not guessing about anything. They are on the offensive. They mapped out their objectives a long time ago and the way in which they were going to achieve them. The period they are in now is that of promoting national revolutions from country to country. We started to lose this war at Yalta, Teheran and Casablanca when we granted all of the concessions that were granted for jumping-off places all through Europe. That is where we began to lose it. These contributions they are making, without using their own forces but by supplying material, advice and that kind of thing, are things that we are going to have to contend with for a long time to come.
As to Europe, I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar this afternoon. We have twelve squadrons over in Europe. From the standpoint of defence for Canada, I believe that we could take six of them back. If we save some money through the process, that is all to the good. I believe that six of them could be back here. Instead of there being a brigade of foot soldiers in Europe, I think the forces there should be, to the extent of at least 75 per cent, armoured forces. I think at this time the real purpose our troops in Europe are serving is that of morale-boosters. If the Russians, with the forces at their disposal, wanted to move there, I do not think there is much there to stop them. However, I do not think they intend to move there; I do not think they have any such intentions. But if they did move, it would be much better to meet them with
Supply-National Defence armour than with foot soldiers. In terms of defence for Canada, I think that these squadrons should be back home. I agree with the observations in the white paper, supported by all of those who have spoken, namely that what we should be thinking about is a mobile striking force; that is, in terms of defence for Canada. The minister himself pointed out that we have a large country with long coast line. We do not know where anything may happen. It could happen anywhere. But we should have in Canada a trained airborne force that we could ship from place to place in a hurry, and it should be at the brigade level. I again agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that at least a brigade of well-trained airborne troops, with sufficient aircraft in the country to move them from one place to another, is something that is absolutely necessary in Canada if we are thinking in terms of defence for Canada. With our population and our resources, as far as a fighting force is concerned that is about all we can do having regard to the international picture that exists today.
This afternoon nobody said much about the reserve army. The last time the defence estimates were before the committee a great deal was said about the reserve army. I myself said a great deal as did the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. At that time, in my opinion, the limiting factor in developing a proper reserve army was the lack of barracks in which to train the men and the lack of equipment. Since that debate took place there has been a big improvement in the barracks and in the equipment. I cannot speak for the whole of the country but I know that in my own end of it there has been a 100 per cent improvement and that, with the improvement in the training facilities-new barracks, in fact, and proper equipment-there are a great many boys interested in taking part in the reserve army today who would not do so previously because there was not available a proper place in which to take instruction. Under our system of voluntary enlistment, I think the reserve army is something that is absolutely necessary. It is the mobilization centre of any future army in Canada. It is the place where we get a great deal of basic training done anyway; and it is much easier to put in the permanent force or in the special force troops who have had some basic training and who have some idea of discipline than it is to pick them raw off the street and out of the ranks of the unemployed and expect them to be good soldiers. I think any money we are spending on the reserve army is well spent. In my end of

Supply-National Defence the country the reserve army has been improved 100 per cent since we last discussed the matter here. I also agree with the statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar this afternoon that the "Maggie" should be re-equipped so that we might have an aircraft carrier on each coast. I think that is necessary not only for training but for many other purposes, and I support him in that contention.
One could go on for a long time in summing up the whole problem, but as I said when I started, it is difficult to criticize the estimates just as it is difficult to estimate what the requirements are going to be with respect to a matter that is purely hypothetical so far as we are concerned. If we were preparing for a war and knew where and when we were going to be hit we could sit down and make our estimates accordingly; but when the initiative is in the other person's hands and he has the world in which to choose his battleground, then we have got to anticipate where and when the outbreak may take place and what type of war it is going to be, and it is pretty hard to sit down and estimate exactly what your requirements are in such circumstances.
I think we have to begin to think in terms of priorities. What are the first priorities? I think our first priority is set out in the white paper, namely, the defence of Canada. Thinking in terms of the defence of Canada, the main emphasis of the Department of National Defence should be on a mobile striking force that can be moved quickly from one section of Canada to the other. I think that is our main concern, and I believe that one-half of our air force in Europe should be brought back to Canada for that purpose. I do not believe we need twelve air force squadrons in Europe as Canada's contribution. I think the minister should give serious consideration to that.
I am convinced that so far as Canada is concerned we should not be thinking about taking part in the kind of show that took place in Korea in the future. We should be building for something bigger than that. We should realize that so far as any of these sideline wars are concerned the battlefield is not in Korea or Indo-China. I think it is pretty nearly time that the free world gave our potential enemy to understand that there is only one battleground and that we are not going to continue to allow ourselves to be dragged into sideline skirmishes in the four corners of the world, skirmishes that only create confusion, at the beck and call of someone whose aim is world conquest. I think it should be clearly understood that
{Mr. Glllis.]

there is only one battleground, and that is the centre from which the whole world disturbance is being promoted.
I believe our build-up should be along these lines, and it should be clearly understood that we recognize what the situation is. If one sifts out what is being said in the United States, I think one can say that that country is beginning to think along those lines. We are in a very difficult position to estimate what our future is going to be. I believe the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich will agree with me that one of the main things a good general will do if he is planning an attack is to choose the battleground upon which he is going to fight. He has a lot in his favour if he can succeed in doing that.
Since the end of the last shooting war we have been in the position of being tossed around like a small boat on the sea because someone who really has a fixed objective, an objective fixed a long time ago, and who has satellites all over the world promoting his aims, is calling the shots in this struggle for world power. It is pretty difficult to sit back on the defensive as we have been doing for a long time and estimate what our future is going to be. First of all, I think we should take care of the defence of Canada and make sure that if anyone does succeed in getting through to us we will be able to give a good account of ourselves. In the second place, we should serve notice on those who are disturbing the peace of the world that they cannot go on forever.
I am not and never have been afraid of Russia starting a world war. She does not have to. She has got the kind of war going today that she wants. This is the kind of thing that she has planned for a good many years. I am convinced she also recognizes that in the countries she has subjugated since the end of the last war there are underground movements waiting for relief. The day an atomic bomb is dropped somewhere in Europe will be the day that Russia will be pushed back within her own borders. She has expanded into Germany. In that part of the world she is like the fly that has captured the fly paper. She is there and she is stuck, and when that paper is disturbed we will have a whole lot of allies in these countries.
That is why I am not afraid of Russia starting a war. She does not need it. She has got the kind of war she wants now. She has been able to drag us to Korea where we have a supply line three or four thousand miles long in order to keep the troops in the field, provide them with munitions and so on. On the

other hand Russia has millions and millions of people to throw in there as cannon fodder, people who can live on rice, and thus she can gain her objective of taking control of the whole of Asia. That is the kind of war she wants. She does not want the other kind.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was only going to make a few rambling remarks. I should like to suggest that the committee on procedure give consideration to making provision for four main speeches in a debate such as this, one from each group in the house. Such speeches would really express the opinions and thinking of the other members of the groups, and when they were over we could get down to the estimates and do the job of getting them cleaned up as quickly as we can.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks on the opening item of the estimates will be concerned chiefly with the Royal Canadian Navy. I think every hon. member is justifiably proud of the Royal Canadian Navy, its great expansion in the last war and the work it performed then and the work it has done since in Korean waters. From any observations I have made of naval personnel since the close of hostilities, I can only say that naval personnel at present and during the last few years are in every way a credit to Canada both at home and abroad.
Like many other hon. members who have already spoken, I thoroughly agree that we cannot discard the so-called conventional weapons at the present time simply because new advances in the field of warfare have been made such as the hydrogen bomb, the atom bomb and so on. I agree with the last member who spoke, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that Russia will probably attempt to hold piecemeal wars here and there, and try to gain control over more territory by the bits and pieces method. We have seen it in Korea, although they did not get too far there. In Indo-China, however, they have been doing fairly well so far. From reports received today, I understand they are very close to Hanoi and are still going. The Russians have been able to succeed in other parts of the world without war, for instance in Czechoslovakia. I rather feel, as many other members have already stated they feel, that this is the kind of thing we are going to have to put up with for a long time.
We may have many localized actions all over the world, and we will not be using nuclear weapons. We shall have to use the more conventional weapons. For that reason, I am quite in accord that the naval forces, with conventional weapons, should be maintained at the highest peak of efficiency. I am
Supply-National Defence glad to see in the estimates put forward by the minister this year that the navy is going to receive its fair share of the funds available. I was pleased also to observe that gracious living is not being taken from the navy. This year 267 chauffeurs are to be maintained as compared with 216 for last year.
The matter with which I should like to deal in some detail concerns the Royal Canadian naval benevolent fund. I mention this because I have received many inquiries about it from naval personnel, so I can only presume that there must be very little general knowledge about the fund. I bring it up at this time because this fund was set up originally by order in council in 1942, P.C. 1067. In due course the fund was incorporated under the dominion Companies Act, and I understand makes an annual report to the Secretary of State. The president of this fund at the moment is an engineering rear admiral, G. L. Stephens, retired. I should like to mention just a few of the directors. They are Commander A. C. Bethune, O.B.E., RCN, retired; Captain J. Jeffrey, O.B.E.; Commander K. Maclachlan; Commodore P. E. Earl; Captain P. B. German; Commander R. P. White, and many others. I just mention those names to illustrate the high qualifications of those who are administering this fund.
The fund has had a rather interesting history, but I intend to deal with it only briefly. I have mentioned already that it was set up in 1942 and was duly incorporated in 1945. I recall very well that at the close of hostilities a signal was sent out by naval service headquarters announcing that the canteen funds of naval ships were to be turned over to this fund. I might say that most of us considered it rather arbitrary at the time because these funds actually were derived from the small profits of ships' canteens and were normally returned to naval personnel on the ships in the form of a bonus when they went on leave or a little extra party at Christmastime if we were in harbour. However, these funds were turned over to the R.C.N. benevolent fund. I believe that at the end of 1945 the fund received $33,000 from the ships that were afloat and $386,000 from shore naval establishments.
Towards the end of 1949 the sum of $1,460,287.25 was contributed to this fund from the prize money that was owing to Canadian naval personnel as a result of the capture of enemy merchant ships during the war. Normally, these moneys would have been distributed to the various former naval personnel, but I am informed that the cost of distributing them to the ex-naval personnel would have been very high and would have used up most of the funds. For this reason, it

Supply-National Defence was turned over to the benevolent fund. I am informed also that there was some little difficulty as to how the money would be paid out, if it had been decided to distribute it. Some of the senior officers thought they should get more than the lower ranks, while other members thought everyone should be paid the same. Since no one could agree, this was one of the contributing reasons for turning the money over to the benevolent fund.
Since that time many other donations have been received by the fund. There have been gifts from private individuals, money from ships' canteens, money from the navy league, and things like that. The last audit statement, December 31, 1953, showed that there was $2,627,509.79 in this fund, largely in dominion government bonds. Since there is all this money in the fund, many people are naturally curious as to who is eligible for assistance. Very briefly and without going into any detail, all members or former members of the naval service are eligible for benefits, as well as their dependents. There is a long description of the dependents, such as widows, wives, children and so on.
The next question is, what type of assistance is given by the fund? Normally, payments out of this fund are apparently in small denominations up to $150 in one class and then up to $300 in another class, and, in certain exceptional cases, over $300. The assistance under this fund is never in the nature of continuing assistance, but rather in the nature of assistance for some unforeseen difficulty such as illness. It is not used for helping people to build homes, to pay business debts or anything like that. I should like to mention that these loans are approved by an executive committee of the board of directors if they are for more than $300. If the loans are under $300, they are approved by one of three claims committees. One of these claims committees looks after the Atlantic provinces, another looks after Ontario, Quebec and the three western provinces and the third looks after British Columbia.
In cases of extreme emergency concerning requests for less than $150, the nearest naval division may authorize payment. The financial statement issued by the fund last year showed that some $629,126 were paid out in grants and $85,281 were advanced to persons in the form of loans. The balance sheet shows an excess of income over expenditures of $11,548. The income consisted of $75,000 from bond interest and $70,000 in donations, funds from ships' canteens and various agencies interested in the navy.
There is one thing that has come up as a result of investigations by the directors of


this fund that directly affects naval personnel and is directly related to these estimates. In a report by Rear Admiral Stephens, who is chairman of this committee, it is pointed out that the directors of this fund are increasingly concerned about applications for assistance from young naval personnel in the active service. Apparently these young people have been getting themselves into debt through buying furniture in an extravagant fashion. They have married while young, and they have not been accustomed to looking after homes. The result has been that they have spent far too much money in trying to keep up with the Joneses, so to speak. Applications of this type have caused the fund considerable worry, and I think the directors of the fund hope that the Minister of National Defence might authorize some sort of brief training course instructing sailors who come to the service in how to run their homes, and how to avoid running up large bills.
The only criticism I have to offer in connection with the benevolent fund is as to the personnel of the board of directors. It would seem to me that it is a bit top-heavy with what might be called the top brass. There are a lot of admirals, captains and commanders, but there do not seem to be any others on that board. It might be helpful if there were one or two able seamen-not too many, perhaps, but just one or two.
In addition to this, people who wish to make applications to the fund might be permitted to make those applications to the local branches of the Legion. The astonishing thing to me is that the ordinary person does not seem to know about it. I feel some effort should be made by the directors of the fund to bring to the attention of the public information as to how one can get at it and how to make application for the benefits it offers. There are a number of naval divisions scattered across Canada, as we know, but they are a long way from the homes of the people requiring assistance. There should be some method of publicizing the fund which, I believe, would be of great assistance to those requiring help from it, and would improve public relations with the fund. Because, from what I have been able to observe, it is being ably run; but because the general public does not know about it, it is not used to the best advantage because people are always suspicious about those things with which they are not familiar.
I should like to leave this point and proceed to another matter. This afternoon the minister mentioned that he was very well satisfied with the naval program, and felt that it was going ahead as well as could be

expected. While there were certain shortcomings, he indicated that he was very pleased with it. This however does not seem to be quite in accordance with the view expressed by Vice-Admiral Mainguy, chief of Canada's naval staff, in a speech delivered not long ago. On March 25 Vice-Admiral Mainguy made a speech in Vancouver. The newspaper article commenting on that speech is as follows:
Vice-Admiral Edmond Mainguy, chief of Canada's naval staff, said Wednesday the navy is "behind" on its 1954 recruiting and expansion program.
He said at a press conference here that the 1954 target is 100 commissioned ships and 21,000 permanent force officers and men.
While the program was behind, recruiting had surged this year, and intake for the permanent force was "slightly more than we can handle" at present, because physical establishments were not big enough to handle the flow.
The shipbuilding program was behind because of a lack of certain technicians, strikes in some cases, and holdups in certain equipment production.
According to the white paper issued by the minister the strength of the navy on March 31, 1954, was 16,955 officers and men, a net increase over last year of 1,409. It is rather interesting to compare these figures with the net increase in previous years. From 1951 to 1952 the net increase in naval personnel was 2,423. In the period from 1952 to 1953 it was 2,041 and in the period 1953 to 1954 it was 1,409.
In other words there has been a steady decrease in the net increase in naval personnel for the last three years. At that rate it seems to me hardly likely that by the end of 1954 the objective of 21,000 officers and men will be reached. The question naturally arises in most people's minds as to the methods used in recruiting, and the advertising costs in connection therewith. In the estimates this year there is a sum of $360,000 as the amount indicated for advertising. Presumably this is for recruiting purposes. I would point out that in the same period last year the amount was $358,000, or about the same as for the coming year.
During the period last year, with a net increase of 1,409 personnel the approximate advertising cost per person on the net increase in personnel was more than $250 each. It would seem to me that at that cost we should have obtained better results. The actual cost of advertising for recruits in the period from 1952 to 1953 was $398,000, for a net increase in naval personnel of 2,041 thus making an actual cost in that period of $188 per person.
As I have said before, advertising costs seem very high, per person, when one considers the number of people coming in. What can we do about it? I would suggest to the
Supply-National Defence minister that he might take certain things into consideration. First of all the obvious thing would be to investigate the type of advertising and publicity that is being used, to see if some improvement can be made. It may be that this is possible, and that we would gain more recruits per advertisement.
On the other hand there is another way that I believe would be more effective-and I have three suggestions in mind. First of all I believe the best results would be obtained if the naval reserve were increased. I would direct the attention of hon. members to page 21 of the minister's white paper where under the heading "Reserve Forces" we find this, in connection with the navy:
A new command was established during the year past to administer and train the R.C.N. (R) and plans are now in progress to increase the total strength of the naval reserve.
Apparently the minister is of the opinion that the reserve force ought to be increased; and I quite agree with him. If the naval reserve is not increasing at the desired rate, one method that might help out would be to make tax free the pay received by members of the naval reserve. I have talked to a number of people who were interested in joining this force, or one of the other services, and they have told me that they would have done so had it not been for the fact that the money they received for their period of training one night a week is subject to tax. This very often puts them in a higher income tax bracket, and they have felt that the amount they have left is not sufficient to warrant the time involved. I have been told on various occasions that if these payments were not taxable they would have been glad to join the reserve units. It is true that some who would join might be somewhat beyond the age of usefulness. But there is certainly an intangible value in having a strong naval reserve. One advantage is that the people see parades; they see the navy turning out. People talk about it, and it is brought to their minds more than it would be in the newspapers or in movie trailers. People can see the name as the personnel come down the street in a church parade, or they have the chance to see them take training courses. That helps to bring the navy to people's minds, not so many advertisements in the paper of two sailors with great big smiles going on leave from a ship, or more often one advertisement which shows sailors with a big smile going back on board after leave, which is very unusual.
Then there is the matter of sea cadets. If you want to get people in the navy you should get them in when the'- are young, because at that time they are more easily
4S38

Supply-National Defence moulded. They are not settled in their ways as some of us are here. When people are young is the best time to get them in the navy. Sea cadets do a wonderful job in this way. When they join the sea cadets they wear a uniform and they get a certain amount of training. It brings the navy home to them. The advantages of the navy can be pointed out to the sea cadets, and when they are through with the sea cadets they can join the navy. When the public sees the sea cadets it also brings the navy to their minds and impresses them with the fact that the navy is a great service to belong to.
Another branch along the same line would be the naval veterans association. Apparently a number of naval veterans associations have sprung up in Canada during the last few years. One was formed in my riding last fall and it has been a great success. A church parade was held, and it brought the navy home to the public. To use the vernacular: "Talk up the navy". It is such things as these that would help in recruiting. It is much more effective than a great deal of advertising. Some of the money that has been spent in advertising could be better used to assist the sea cadets and the small branches of the naval veterans association. If that were done the recruiting program in the long run would be much more successful.
The next item I should like to touch on is the matter of some of our new ships. Last fall I, along with other hon. members, had the opportunity of seeing some of our new destroyer type of escort ships which are in the process of construction. From my little knowledge gained in past years I would say that these ships appear to me to be well designed by Canadian personnel, I understand, and are indeed a credit to the navy. However, I agree with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that these ships are a little expensive for the type of work they will be doing. Perhaps some other method, as the hon. member pointed out this afternoon, would be better. The question also arises in my mind: Is the construction of those ships proceeding as fast as it should? This afternoon the minister said that construction was proceeding as fast as similar construction in other countries, but I do not think he intimated it was proceeding as fast as he would like to see it. I am informed that shortly before last Christmas there was a hold-up in the construction of those new destroyer escort type ships and this hold-up was due to shortages of materials that had to be ordered from abroad. When the minister replies he may enlighten us on whether


any hold-up in construction has taken place, and whether construction has resumed or is still held up.
The information I received is apparently substantiated by the chief of naval staff in the speech that I referred to earlier. He said that the shipbuilding program was behind because of lack of certain technicians and was held up for certain equipment production. These remarks of the chief of the naval staff seem to substantiate the statement made to me that the construction of those ships was not proceeding as fast as it should.
Another type of ship that I had the opportunity to observe at the same time last fall was the new type of minesweeper which was under construction. This minesweeper, unlike the ones used in the last war, was designed largely for minesweeping purposes. It seemed to be an excellent ship indeed with the one exception. A gun was mounted on the ship aft the funnel. It appeared to me to be a type of gun known as a pom-pom. In the last war those guns were not particularly effective against enemy aircraft, and I doubt very much whether this gun would have very much effect against a modern jet aircraft, which certainly travels a great deal faster than the aircraft used in the last war. I made some inquiries at the time and it was indicated to me that this gun was placed there largely for morale purposes and not for any destructive purposes. That is all very well. It is pleasant to keep up morale, but when you have to put heavy gun mountings away above the water line on the ship you have increased the amount of ballast that has to be built in in almost geometric proportion. It would seem that if those ships are going to be used for minesweeping they would be much better protected by supporting aircraft than by a single pom-pom.
There are two other items which I should like to touch on before concluding. The first is the matter of officer training in the navy. This matter is of some interest to me because during the last war I was at one time largely connected with officer training. I understand that at the present time for the first two years the embryo naval officers, along with embryo officers from the other services, attend those tri-service colleges and they all get the same training. That is all very fine, and it may have certain economic advantages. It may serve to get one service more familiar with the activities of another, but on the other hand I wonder whether it is just the wise thing. In the minister's white paper, which he set out very well, he said

that the main object of the Canadian navy is to protect convoys and the secondary purpose is harbour defence. Accordingly the inference is that we are not going to be concerned with large combined operations in landings, and so on, as the British navy and the United States navy are. Our purpose is designed peculiarly for convoy work, as we did in the last war. If that is so, it would not indicate that this tri-service training is particularly necessary. If we are not going to be in combined operations, what is the purpose? In my opinion this tri-service training that we are undergoing at the present time causes a great many things to be sacrificed that are peculiar to the navy. I do not use the word "peculiar" in the sense of being strange; but it is in particular, shall I say, the habits and customs, the methods of discipline, all of which tend to engender pride in one's service and increase morale. I think there is a great tendency to lose some of this in having the three services all training together, and nobody knowing whether he is fish or flesh, so to speak. I mention that for the minister's consideration. Has the tri-service college worked out as well as it was supposed to?
A matter that I should like to touch on, which does not concern the navy, was mentioned by the minister this afternoon, namely, the joint United States-Canadian network of radar defence stations in northern Canada. To date we have not received any figures as to what it has cost. It is my understanding that these sums are of a confidential and secret nature. There is very little doubt that the costs of those radar defence stations are very high indeed. It cannot be otherwise. Every hon. member will agree that Canada should do her bit in helping to defend this continent. We are very glad to do our share. There seems little doubt in my mind that these radar defence stations are really far more for the protection of the United States than they are for the protection of Canada. There are far more targets in the United States which would be apt to be the subject of H or A-bomb attacks than there are in Canada. But the minister has not told us what these stations are going to cost and what relative proportion of payment has been worked out. Is the United States going to pay the entire cost or are they going to pay only a part?

I had heard rumours to that effect, Mr. Chairman, although I did not realize they had been made official. However, it would seem to me that since the population of the United States is more than ten times that of Canada and their wealth and resources are vastly superior, and perhaps 10 times more than that of Canada-possibly, Mr. Chairman, I had better correct that statement. I would say that American resources and wealth are considerably more than 10 times that of Canada and her population is certainly more than 10 times that of Canada. It would therefore seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that Canada's share should not be one-third but perhaps nearer to one-tenth. As I said earlier, we want to pay our share but we do not want to be goats for the United States. These defences help the United States as much as or more than they assist Canada, and I cannot see why a country smaller in both actual wealth and population should have to pay such a high percentage.
It is true that we have vast wealth and resources which are as yet undeveloped, but at the present time American resources and wealth are infinitely superior to our own and I cannot feel that we should pay one-third of the cost of these stations. It seems to me to be quite ridiculous.
I know these matters are international in character and that we have to play along with the United States. In fact, I would be the first to agree with that, but I still feel that Canada is paying far too much in this regard, and I hope the minister, perhaps through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, might be able to make some other arrangement in future whereby we can pay a little less.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I wish to remark that I do not share the optimism expressed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South when he suggested that modern atomic and H-bombs were so horrible that they would probably never be brought into use and that we could work on that assumption. I can well imagine that after the terrible slaughter at the battle of Crecy it was observed by the people on the scene, and the opinion held by many thereafter, that another war would be impossible when one contemplated the horrible slaughter caused by the blunderbuss against which there was no defence.
I therefore think we would be deluding ourselves and falling into a state of mind which

Supply-National Defence might give us a false sense of security if we were to suppose that that was so.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I noted with satisfaction in the introduction to the white paper which was tabled by the minister the other day these words:
It is appropriate now to provide the fullest possible information on our defence activities and plans in order that this program can be understood in the light of Canada's over-all defence policy.
Having read that, I am going on the assumption that the minister will welcome a close questioning on the activities of the Department of National Defence, and I assume that the more penetrating the questions are the happier the minister will be.
Now, the question of national defence in this country has become a colossal one. It is a department which spends much more of the national budget than any other department, and indeed a very large proportion of our total budget is now spent on defence.
Our defence effort has many new phases. There is the defence of this continent and this country; there is our contribution to NATO; there are the three services to be considered; the reserve forces, and the question of research on methods of defence, which is now the responsibility of the defence research board; and there are many other phases in this vast program of national defence. I therefore consider, Mr. Chairman, that it is impossible and perhaps inadvisable for me to attempt to give even a cursory view of the whole question of national defence because by so doing I could only skim the surface in the 40 minutes at my disposal. Therefore, I intend to confine my remarks to two subjects only which are of special interest to me. However, since it is practically ten o'clock, I do not think I should continue meantime but should ask you, Mr. Chairman, to call it ten o'clock.
