Mr. Chairman, when I was interrupted I was saying that there were two subjects to which I wanted to confine my attention. One of them is the reserve forces of the army and navy in the province from which I come, and in the course of my remarks in that connection I will probably be paying particular attention to the reserve forces in my own riding.
We in Prince Edward Island are very proud of the history and record of our reserve forces which have been built up over the last 150 years. They have a very proud record of service both in peace and in many wars. I think you will pardon me if, in that connection, I quote briefly from the Prince Edward Island magazine for April, 1900, over 50 years ago. Even at that time a record of excellent service by the reserve forces of that province had already been built up. At page 40 in this article I note the following:
In 1812, we find the "garden province" sending her sons to battle in the war of that date. In that year 100 volunteers left Queen's wharf on one of H.M. ships-of-war en route to the scene of conflict.
And so on. Then again they go on to say:
In the Crimean war, quite a number of Islanders fought in the British ranks; some went from the Island and others enlisted from different parts of the world. In fact, wherever Britain's battles were being fought, whether in the Crimea, beneath the walls of China, or the battlefields of Europe and

America, there might be found the sons of the "Garden of the Gulf" fighting valiantly for their sovereign and the empire.
I cite that merely to point out that it has been traditional in my province for young men to take a keen interest in the reserve forces and to serve in them if at all possible. They automatically considered that service to be one of their responsibilities. In that connection may I say this. Even before the province entered confederation it had a very fine record of service in that connection. In order that my remarks will not be classified merely as an opinion, I should again like to read a quotation. I am quoting now from the report of the inspecting field officer of militia for the year 1868. He had this to say:
I have dwelt at some length on this portion of the militia because it is the effective force of the island, and too much attention cannot be given to the maintenance of its efficiency as it appears a matter of certainty that the Imperial troops are no longer to hold garrison here. The "material" is unexceptionable and only requires steady instruction, good organization and discipline to render it a force second to none. They are most eager to obtain the means of training, and were the staff of instructors twice as numerous as it is, it would be insufficient to meet all the demands made upon it. The Queen's County Regiment of Volunteer Militia is well commanded by competent field officers.
He goes on to say, in that connection, that during that year 9,178 men in the reserves received instruction. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, in that year in the one county alone, with a population of only 45,000, the colony had 5,213 trained reserves before confederation.
I have a purpose in making these rather ancient quotations, and I hope it will become more evident as I go along. It goes almost without saying that in the later wars-the Boer war, the first and second great wars and now more recently the Korean war- recruiting and volunteering for active service have been highly satisfactory indeed in the island province; and I believe this situation is owing to the fine record of service achieved and the interest which has been kept up by the reserve units over the years. During the South African war there were 75 men who volunteered, mostly from Prince Edward Island. That is not a large figure but it is a large percentage in relation to the population, considering the numbers who saw service in South Africa. In the first world war there were almost 4,000 recruits in the army alone from that province or who were recruited in that province, not taking into account men who served in the navy and men who enlisted in the neighbouring provinces for service in that war. In the last war the total enlistment was much greater.
Supply-National Defence The army had about 6,500, the air force had nearly 2,000 and the navy had 1,500. That makes a total of approximately 10,000. That does not take into account considerable numbers of men from that province who served in the merchant navy and who enlisted in the neighbouring provinces for service.
I think that this record is not accidental, Mr. Chairman. As I have already stated, I think one of the reasons for it was the fine degree of interest in military service which has been kept up in that province over the years by the active reserve units of the army and latterly of the navy in that province. Between the two wars these units included the Prince Edward Island Highlanders, the P.E.I. light horse, two old established medium batteries of artillery and other units such as a company of signals, medical corps and so on. Since the second world war the tradition of these regiments is now being carried on by the P.E.I. R.E.C.C.E. regiment, the 28th light anti-aircraft regiment, a unit of signals, a medical corps unit and so forth. The R.C.N.V.R. reserves in that province have the record of being one of the earliest units of the R.C.N.V.R. organized in Canada. I think it was either the first or the second unit. During the last war, personnel who had served in that reserve unit created a proud record of service for the area, especially the city of Charlottetown. In the last war there were over 100 commissioned officers serving in the Canadian navy from the small city of Charlottetown with a population of only about 15,000. I think that result amply justifies many times over any expenditure which may have been made on behalf of that small naval reserve unit before the last war.
I should now like to consider for a few minutes the difficulties under which these reserve units are working. Last year I put on the order paper a question with regard to the armouries in Charlottetown. It was a very simple question and read as follows:
When were the armouries in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, built?
I received this rather amazing answer: No information. The reason there is no information is that the armouries in Charlottetown are so old that you would have to dig into the archives to find out when they were built. I therefore took it upon myself to attempt to supply some of the information. I find that the armouries in Charlottetown were built by the colonial government well prior to Prince Edward Island entering confederation. In the report of the inspecting
4942	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence officer of militia for 1867-and he was Colonel A. Douglas Smith-I find this statement:
Three drill sheds have been erected. Their erection was a matter of absolute necessity and will confer positive important benefits on the inhabitants of Charlottetown, Summerside and Georgetown.
That was the beginning of the present Charlottetown armouries. I find in the public accounts for the same year a reference to warrants which were paid toward the construction of that drill hall to the amount of 1,671 pounds, 11 shillings and 11 pence. That will give some indication of the age of the building. It is an old, inadequate wooden building. True, there have been some modifications and additions.
In that connection I find that the armouries, which are now called the "drill hall"-the two terms are synonymous-were opened on the 15th of January, 1867. A new drill hall at the west end of Kent street was opened by the commander in chief, Lieutenant Governor George Dundas. I find too that the drill hall was widened a little bit on the west side prior to the first great war. Here is another interesting note:
The new artillery orderly rooms facing Government Pond were opened on the evening of the 8th of April, 1897.
When anything in my province is less than 55 years old it is new as far as accommodation for the reserve force is concerned. I should like you to pay special attention to this point, that these rooms were largely paid for by the officers of the artillery units themselves out of their personal incomes. I believe that should give the committee some indication of the inadequacy of the accommodation provided for the reserve forces in the capital city of Prince Edward Island. Prior to confederation a wave of interest in national defence seemed to sweep over the colony. No doubt this was partly due to the threat of war between the colonies and the United States. Possibly the fervour of patriotic zeal may have been fanned by the excitement caused just a few years prior by the "Charge of the Light Brigade", but in any event the colony saw fit to build a drill hall and we are still getting by with substantially the same building.
I think I should also refer to the accommodation provided for the naval reserve unit, now known as H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte. As I have already said, it has a very fine record of service but it is housed in a building which is over 100 years old, a building which was first used as a furniture factory, then subsequently as a candy factory, then for a while as an emergency hospital for the insane because of a


serious fire in that institution, then was vacant for a number of years, and then H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte fell heir to it. It is rented from the provincial government at considerable expense, and the building is utterly unsuitable for the use to which it is put. It is in such bad condition that I understand it is not safe to allow more than 60 people on the second floor at any time because it may collapse.
It was also found impossible to instal the training equipment supplied for the division because it was too heavy to be set up in the building. I am happy to have read that the commanding officer of the naval reserve units, Commodore Adams, recently inspected that division, and it is referred to in the press as follows:
A strong recommendation for better training facilities for H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte will be made by Commodore Kenneth F. Adams, C.D., R.C.N., commanding officer, naval division, Hamilton, Ontario.
I am confident that this strong recommendation will go through, and when it does I hope it will be sympathetically dealt with because I think the minister will recognize that I am not pleading for any special handout for my riding. Neither am I pleading for any unjustified expenditure of public funds. I think that adequate facilities for the reserve units in the city of Charlottetown are completely justified. It would be good business and in the long run would effect economies in defence expenditures.
That of course is predicated on the supposition that in the future pattern of defence there is a place for the reserve forces. I feel strongly that there is. I should like the minister to clarify the position of our reserve forces and the role they will play in national defence in the years ahead. I think there is considerable demand throughout the country that the role of our reserve forces be clarified so that not only they but the general public will know what the policy is regarding them.
There is another facility used by the reserve units in my province to which I want to refer very briefly. It is the rifle range just outside of Charlottetown at Squaw Point. I understand that the butts there are being eroded by the sea and it is necessary either to move them or to protect them by some sort of sea wall. I hope that the need for maintaining a standard rifle range in that area will be recognized and that at an early time the required attention will be given to that project. That is all I want to say in that connection except to appeal to the minister to see that this ancient injustice is rectified. I do not want to make any special criticism of the present government because the facilities

of the reserve forces are so unsatisfactory inasmuch as it is the fault not only of this government but of every government for the last 50 years that the accommodation for the reserve forces in my province is so inadequate.
I want to turn for a few moments to an entirely different subject. I refer to aircraft procurement for the Royal Canadian Air Force. In the white paper tabled by the minister the other day there is the statement that several CF-100 all-weather squadrons are already operating in Canada. I should like some clarification as to exactly what "several" means. I know that the dictionary meaning of "several" is anything more than two. But by using that term, people might be led to believe that it is considerably more than two. I have a suspicion that the number is three, and I should like the minister to say definitely whether or not my assumption on that point is correct.
With regard to the equipment with which these squadrons are supplied, and the people of our air force squadrons as well, I note this statement in the white paper:
A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited has completed delivery of the Canuck (CF-100) Mk 3 aircraft and delivery of Mk 4 version has started. The Canuck is powered with the Canadian designed and built Orenda engine and will include a new type of autopilot which will be coupled to the fire control system.
Then, a little further on the white paper states:
Canadair Limited of Cartierville, near Montreal, is making deliveries of Sabre 5 (F-86) aircraft with the Orenda series 10 engine, according to schedule. The latest model, the Sabre 6, also has an airframe similar to that of the American built F-86E but will be powered with the Orenda series 14 engine. It will be superior in performance to the Sabre 5. Sabre 5 and 6 aircraft will meet R.C.A.F. commitments overseas and will eventually replace the Sabre 2s which are now flown operationally by the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe.
I have no desire, Mr. Chairman, to cast any reflection on the excellent work that has been done by the designers of the Orenda engine or any other designers and engineers concerned with the development of the Orenda engine and the CF-100. My first concern, and my chief concern, is to do anything I can to ensure that the R.C.A.F. is equipped with the best possible equipment. I am especially anxious that it will be equipped with the best possible fighting equipment. In that way, the Canadian taxpayers will get the best value for their defence dollar. After all, money which might be spent for equipment which is obsolescent or even obsolete, or too little or too late, is a complete waste. In this connection we should set ourselves the highest possible standards because nothing but the best is
Supply-National Defence good enough in the position that we find ourselves in so far as the aerial defence of North America and our contribution to NATO defence are concerned.
In that spirit I want to draw to the attention of the committee what I consider to be the nub, the starting point of any fighting equipment for an air force. I refer to engines. In that connection I think my thoughts are very well expressed in an editorial appearing in Flight magazine for April, 1954, on page 445. They have this to say:
Though the statement may seem a truism, engines really are very important-more so, in certain aspects, than the aircraft they drive. A good modern aero engine is an immense national asset; it is the result not only of a multi-million-pound development but the focal point of aircraft development programs costing many millions more. Everything that is done by the aircraft of the future- stratospheric reconnaissance, short-haul transport, supersonic combat or jungle warfare with helicopters-will be vitally dependent upon the provision of engines of the right sort at the right time. All kinds of engines are needed: for fighters, the requirements are thrust, high-altitude performance, low frontal area, reliability, economy and durability, approximately in that order of importance; . . .
Now, this article goes on to make this observation. They have been speaking about the requirements, the vast requirements necessary, such as electronic computing equipment and that sort of thing, in the development of new types of aircraft engines. The development of a modern engine is really a colossal undertaking. This article observes that in the United States great use is made of modern equipment of this sort, and then goes on to say:
With such tools, there is no reason to doubt that our position as the world's top-ranking designer of aero engines will be maintained. Already our gas turbines are in production, under licence, in Sweden, Switzerland, Italy, France, Belgium, Argentina and the U.S.A.-and, without a licence, in Russia.
I might add that the Avon engine is now in production in Australia.
Production, too, is going very well, and more than one aircraft factory is probably finding storage of delivered engines almost an embarrassment. (The same sort of situation has, we hear, arisen across the Atlantic.) In fact, our superpriority engines-the Avon, Sapphire, Olympus . . . etc.

are without exception progressing well and showing every indication of forming the backbone of our civil and military power for years to come.
I would be the last, Mr. Chairman, to prejudge any Canadian effort in the field of design or production of aircraft engines. No one will be more delighted than I will be if the minister can inform the committee that Canada has already the lead in that connection, and that the great advances which have been made since the last published figures put Canada in the forefront in this field. But I am not confident that is so. I should
4944	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence like, however, to refer to a comparison of published information regarding modern aircraft engines.
The Orenda is a good engine. It was well designed but it has taken considerable time to get it into large-scale production. It should be remembered that this is a highly competitive field and that time is of the essence. One must not only design good engines, but one must get them into production quickly or they will be obsolescent. As has already been noted, the main characteristics of interest with regard to aircraft engines are thrust, that is to say the power of the jet engine, frontal area, fuel economy and so on. Those are the things of paramount importance.
I should like to put on the record some figures relating to modern British aircraft engines. The Bristol Olympus, for example, is 40 inches in diameter, has a weight of roughly 3,500 pounds. It has a thrust of 9,750 pounds and has a specific fuel consumption of -766. I will not take up the time of the committee to quote other figures with regard to the Sapphire and the Avon, because they are roughly in the same bracket.
I do not want any comparison to be considered unfair. I believe the comparisons I make are as nearly true as they can be made. I note that the engines I have already named are now powering, without exception, some of the best aircraft in the world, so far as operational aircraft are concerned. Among them are the Vulcan, which is powered with an Olympus. And that engine, by the way, is being manufactured in the United States by Curtiss-Wright, and I believe also by Buick. Others of these aircraft are the Vulcan, the Gloster Javelin, the Victor, the Hawker Hunter, Republic F-84F, Martin Canberra, the de Havilland-110 all-weather fighter, the de Havilland Comet 3, the Canberra, and the Australian version of the Sabre.
When one contrasts those figures with the latest data available on the Orenda engine he finds that, as compared with these British engines with a thrust up to 9,500 pounds, the Orenda has a thrust of 6,500, at least in the earlier marks. The really important thing of course with modern aircraft engine design is the specific fuel consumption. To put it in everyday parlance: How far will you go on a gallon? Because the higher the fuel consumption, the lower will be the radius of action, and the less will be the range of the aircraft in which the power plant is installed.
In the case of the Olympus, the specific fuel consumption in pounds per hour of pounds thrust is -766; in the case of the Sapphire it is '85; with the Avon it is [DOT]84, and with the Orenda it is one. That is a colossal difference. Those early marks of


Orenda compared very unfavourably with the most up-to-date British designs. The only consolation I find in these figures is a brief reference to the later marks of the Orenda.

speechtext:
That is true. I have tried to make my comparisons as fair as possible. For instance, I have taken the Avon engine which is now powering the Australian version of the Sabre. I will admit that some of the most up-to-date aircraft I have mentioned are just coming into production in England. They have super-priority, and they will be the aircraft with which the forces of Great Britain and of other countries will be equipped in the very near future.
The consolation I find in these figures is that, having reference to the later models of the Orenda-I refer to mark 11 and mark 14, with the after-burner-we get a thrust of as high as 8,500 pounds, and I believe the specific fuel consumption is well under one.
I just wish to make the point, though, that there are two considerations to be met. One of these is whether national prestige in the aircraft industry is of first importance, or whether the best possible equipment for our air force, regardless of where it can be obtained, is of first importance.
In that connection I will grant you that, if at all possible, the equipment should be manufactured on this continent. But that is already being done. Some of the most up to date engines are already being manufactured in the United States, under licence and, as I have already said, in France, Australia, and the Argentine and many other countries. Canada is the sole exception to the manufacture of advanced designs of British aircraft engines, under licence. I am just a bit doubtful if the fact that we are that exception can be entirely justified. I would ask the minister to reassure us that we are following the correct course in that regard.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: We are producing the goods in the most efficient and formidable fighting aircraft in the world today in quantity production.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that. But I am thinking not only of today but of the very near future. Because

we know that modern aircraft become obsolete extremely rapidly in this very competitive age. I imagine this question has been carefully considered. We know that the Minister of Defence Production has already said that if the Minister of National Defence asks him for a gold-plated piano, it is his duty to supply it. I would hope that if this is considered justified-and I am not putting it in the same bracket, at all-consideration might be given to equipping some of the aircraft made in Canada with the most up to date and the best engines in the world, under licence, if they are not already designed in Canada for that purpose.
I have almost reached the conclusion of my remarks, and the time at my disposal has almost expired. But I do note that in the white paper the minister has tabled it is observed that members of Canada's armed forces are serving on the staffs of nine principal NATO headquarters and large agencies, including Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe, commonly known as SHAPE, as well as Headquarters Allied Air Forces Central Europe-and several others.
As already noted, Canada is contributing a very large air element to the NATO defence of Europe. I am just wondering where Canada fits in, from a military point of view, with regard to the tactical use of the air force, if war should come. I am wondering if consideration has already been given to the possibility of, if not command of the air force, a position of deputy commander, and that if for a time such position might be held by a Canadian. I am curious to know if that suggestion has been made and, if it has been, how it has been looked upon by the Canadian government. Because if that suggestion were ever followed it would give Canada an appropriate command of the situation to which it is contributing so heavily in armament. And when I say "heavily", I mean that we are spending a great deal in national defence, especially in connection with the equipping of our air force.
In connection with the Orenda CF-100 project, I think it is fair to say that more money has already been spent on that-and I am not suggesting it was not justified-than it will cost to build the St. Lawrence seaway. Therefore, I think it is only fair that we should examine very carefully all expenditures which are made in this connection. I have some other questions, but I shall ask them when the particular items are up later on. At this point I shall conclude my remarks on the first item.

I have listened with great interest to the eloquent plea of the hon. member for Queens on behalf of
Supply-National Defence the need for a new armoury at Charlottetown. I hope it will be possible at the same time to provide an armoury for St. John's, Newfoundland. Charlottetown has at least an armoury, old though it may be. St. John's, unfortunately, has none. I would therefore strongly urge that the minister give favourable consideration to the establishment of an armoury at St. John's, one that will be worthy of the historic traditions of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment.

speechtext: Just in case I have been misunderstood I should like to correct one thing in connection with the armouries in Charlottetown. Perhaps I did not make myself clear, but they were not built by the federal government; they were built by the colonial government and given to the dominion government at confederation.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has been listening to a lot of speeches this afternoon and this evening. I have not got a speech prepared but I do have a couple of questions I should like to ask him. Perhaps he can deal with them this evening. The first has to do with the policy of the R.C.A.F., with regard to commercial work. I got a return, which was dated April 13 of this year, in answer to several questions. The questions which are apropos are as follows:
During 1953, did the Royal Canadian Air Force engage in any flying within Canada except for the Department of National Defence or other government departments?
If so,
(a)	For whom:
(b)	What types of aircraft were employed, and how many hours on each type;
(c)	How many passengers and pounds of cargo were carried in each case?
Was any remuneration received for such flying?
(a)	If so, from whom and how much in each case;
(b)	What was the rate charged per mile, per hour or per ton mile?
The answers to these questions showed that the air force had been doing commercial flying, and in particular they had flown for the Iron Ore Company of Canada a matter of 181-15 hours and carried 121 passengers and about one million pounds of cargo. The actual figures were 989,432 pounds. They had been paid for this work as follows:
The Iron Ore Company of Canada paid $39,473.52 calculated at the rate of .42 cents per ton mile and $1.56 per ferry air mile.
I understand that there were civilian flying companies in a position to do that work. The minister should explain why the R.C.A.F. was in effect competing with civilian flying companies in work which was obviously of a civilian nature. I am informed that such a policy is directly the opposite of the policy adopted in the United States. I believe that
4946	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the United States air force fosters the development of civilian aviation and in fact employs civilian firms to do some of the United States air force flying in the continental United States but not abroad. Overseas the flying for the United States air force is all done by air force planes.
There seems to be a difference of policy in the two countries. The United States believes in taking every step to build up a healthy aviation industry; whereas Canada, in this instance at least, has been interfering with the civil aviation industry. I believe the only way we can hope to maintain and build up a strong civil aviation industry in this country is not to have their potential work taken by the R.C.A.F. Certainly parliament is not voting funds for the R.C.A.F. with the idea that air force planes will be used on civilian work.
I understand also that the air service to the meteorological stations of the government is being done by the R.C.A.F., and presumably that comes under the defence vote. It seems that some argument could be made for that flying being done by the civilian companies. Why would it not be a wise plan to encourage civilian companies by giving them work of this type?
Then, there is the flying in connection with the ice patrols on the Atlantic coast and out of the port of Churchill on the opening of navigation. Apparently this work is done by the R.C.A.F. Why could it not be done by civilian flyers? It does seem to me that here is a way in which civilian aviation in Canada could be fostered, if a proper government policy were adopted. I have one other question on another matter. I wonder whether the minister would deal with these questions of the R.C.A.F. doing what is in essence civilian flying?

speechtext:
I do not know what the purpose of it is. The information might be more readily and more accurately given, no doubt, when the item for the air force comes up for consideration, but I can speak now from my recollection of what happened many months


ago. The Labrador iron ore development had a deadline to meet that was in the interests of the national defence of Canada and of the United States. I was told by the general manager of the concern that they did not have an airlift to meet their deadline. I was told that over the long distance telephone. I asked the R.C.A.F. if they had an airlift. They said that by diverting aircraft from other important air work they could do it, if necessary. I said: "Clear this with the air transport board and make sure that we are not treading on anyone's toes." They did. We carried out the airlift. It was carried out successfully in the national interest. It was not any part of the national policy except to get on with the job of completing the Labrador iron ore development in the time that was necessary. If, in consequence of that, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has any complaints, then I shall be glad to answer them when the item in the estimates comes up for the air force. My recollection, speaking as I say from telephone conversations, is that there were only two of them, one from the general manager of the company, and one to the chief of the air staff. When the request was made the general manager of the company said he had no other airlift available and said he had cleared the other air commitments. I informed the chief of the air staff that he must clear this with the air transport board. He did that, and he provided the airlift. I do not know why anyone should have any reason to complain.
With regard to the supply of weather stations, there you go into a very complicated field in which you have to have the men, the special types of equipment, the gasoline and the aircraft capable of doing long range flights. Generally speaking, with the long range operation we find it has been a good thing to employ R.C.A.F. aircraft.
But finally, in answer to the hon. member, may I say that it is just as important that the R.C.A.F. should have and be maintained in the capacity to deliver long lift air transport operations as much as it is to maintain civilian transport companies. Our idea is that we work together. We do not compete, and where a civilian operates and the job can be done by a civilian we never enter into it except in circumstances of extreme urgency such as I have described.

speechtext: Does the minister say that the United States air force is not now engaging civilian firms to do some work for the air force in the United States?

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: There is no difference at all. It the United States air force is the only air force to provide an airlift on an essential operation in the national interest they carry out that operation, but if there is a civilian source to do a civilian job then they leave it to the civilians, just as we do. We employed civilians on the airlift to Korea and in fact the C.P.A. has done a magnificent job supported by us. We employ civilians all over the place when they are the best agency to do the job, in the same fashion as the Americans.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: What about the ice patrol, and the patrol out of Churchill?

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: I would have to look up the record about that. I have not heard anything about it except for some details a few months ago, and I would have to look into the facts. But I would think that was probably an operation which could best be conducted ordinarily by service aircraft because they would have to do a patrol in any event for surveillance purposes.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: But I suggest to the minister that in the case of the Iron Ore Company of Canada it is going pretty far to act on the basis of a call from the general manager of that company.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: No, no! We cleared it with the air transport board which has control over civil aviation and they assured us that it was the right thing to do and we did not undertake-

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: I understand that at least one member of the air transport board protested against that and considered it an unwise policy-

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: Then you must talk to him.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: Whether the air transport board approved that or not is not very important. The question is-

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: What was important was to get the job done.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: But it is not the minister's business to use the R.C.A.F. to get civilian work done, and why the Iron Ore Company of Canada should be in such a great hurry to meet a deadline when they are a civilian firm opening up their own iron mine I simply cannot understand. I do not see why the manager of that firm or any other firm should be able to pick up the phone, call the minister, and ask him to turn over R.C.A.F. planes to carry freight for them. I suggest, Mr. Chairman-

speechtext: I would suggest that you both cannot have the floor at the same time. If the minister is not rising on a point of order I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra should be allowed to complete his statement.

speechtext: I thought he had finished.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: Well I was still on my feet talking and I do not see how the minister came to the conclusion I was finished.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext: At this time of night you can come to any conclusion.

maintopic: ALLEGED INFRACTIONS OF PACKING REGULATIONS BY THREE TORONTO FIRMS
speechtext:
I do not finish quite that easy. I do suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's answer shows that the government was wrong in this case. Why should an official of the Iron Ore Company of Canada be able to ring the minister and say, "Here, Mister, send me R.C.A.F. transports. I want to get some cement"-or whatever it was-"carried from Sept lies into the district where we are developing a mine, and I want to get it done in a hurry. I have a civilian deadline to meet." The minister acts on that and turns a North Star over and now comes in here and tries to justify that on the ground that it was for the defence of Canada. I suggest that this is really going beyond all reason, and it is all rather far-fetched.
I merely bring this up to point out to the minister the need for being a good deal more careful in the use of the R.C.A.F. for civilian purposes. I know he is very proud of the R.C.A.F., and quite properly so. We are all proud of it and we have very good reason to be not only for what it did in the second world war, but also during the postwar period, and of course the exploits of our airmen during the first world war. But the time has surely come in Canada with the development of the north country, and the attempt to push our borders in that direction, to do everything possible to foster civilian flying. After all, that has been the basis of the R.C.A.F., and Canada has been the leader in the development of northern flying. Here is a case where a company should have been told to look after its own business, hire planes on its own, and not come running to the Minister of National Defence in order to obtain R.C.A.F. planes to do work so obviously of a civilian nature.
